Overview

A working reference for solid rocket motor mechanical design — — of tools, data and the reasoning behind them. Nothing here needs a network.

PREDICTOR LAB — PREDICTIONS LIVE APART FROM THE REFERENCE DATA Work package estimator for hours and cost from your own history, Weibull reliability, Monte Carlo uncertainty, regression with prediction intervals, and the general predictor bench. Kept outside the eight phases so a fitted model is never mistaken for an allowable.

The route through

The zones are ordered by when you use them, from understanding the material through to releasing the drawing. You will not work through them in order every time — but this is roughly the sequence a component actually follows.

THE ONE-PARAGRAPH DRAWING PHILOSOPHY A drawing is a contract, not a picture. Every dimension and note should answer one question: “how will the inspector accept or reject this?” If a requirement can't be measured, it can't be enforced. Dimension the function, tolerance only as tight as the function needs, and state the standard you're working to (in the UK, that's BS 8888 in the title block).
FASTEST WAY TO USE THIS SITE Ctrl/Cmd-F works on every page, and the Standards page has its own live filter. Each design guide ends with a copy-ready drawing callout in a dashed box.

ZONE 11

Material selector

Pick a family, tick what the part needs, then sort any column. — materials covering aluminium, titanium, nickel and cobalt superalloys, stainless, high-strength case steels, magnesium, refractories, carbon/ablatives, composites and polymers.

Selection chart

An Ashby-style property chart over all — materials. Choose an application preset or build your own: pick the two properties that matter, decide which families to include, apply limits, then overlay a performance index to rank the survivors and draw its selection line.

HOW TO READ THE SELECTION LINE With an index active on its natural axes, the dashed lines are contours of constant index value — every material on a given line performs identically for that requirement. Moving the line towards the top-left improves performance, so anything lying above and left of the bold line beats your current best candidate. This is the whole point of an Ashby chart: it shows you not just the winner, but everything within reach of it, and what you would trade to get there.

DATA PROVENANCE — READ BEFORE YOU TRUST A RANKING Values are typical room-temperature figures for screening and ranking, not design allowables. Strength is 0.2% proof for metals, failure stress for ceramics and ablatives, and unidirectional fibre-direction failure stress for composites — so the three are not directly comparable, and the ranking table now says which applies. Fracture toughness is indicative only: it varies strongly with condition, orientation and section thickness. Temperature-dependent properties are quoted at ambient unless the material exists only hot. Take design values from the governing material specification, an allowables source such as MMPDS or CMH-17, or your own test data.

Ranking & comparison

Top candidates by the selected index. Tick up to four to compare them side by side.

DESIGN NOTES — DECISIONS, TRAPS AND CHECK SEQUENCES
MATERIAL SELECTION — IN ONE LINE Design to the allowable at temperature, for the exposure time, in the load direction — never to room-temperature typical yield.

The selector's job is to stop designs being sized on the wrong number. For anything that sees heat, the governing figure is strength at temperature after the actual exposure time.

Screening data

Yield is the specification minimum for a common product form. Retention is an approximate fraction of room-temperature yield on short exposure. Screening only — pull the real curve and basis before any analysis.

AlloyMin yield MPa150°C300°C500°Cρ g/cm³

TRAP Precipitation-hardened steels over-age permanently above their ageing temperature, and 17-4PH also embrittles with long exposure in roughly the 300–450°C range. Neither recovers on cooling. Keep service temperature well below the ageing temperature, or pick a different alloy.

Selection order that works

  1. Filter on temperature capability for the exposure duration, not the peak alone.
  2. Filter on environment — galvanic pairing and stress-corrosion susceptibility.
  3. Then optimise on specific strength. Doing this first is how 7075 ends up in a hot joint.
  4. Check the product form. A forging allowable is not your allowable if you machine from plate.
WATCH High-strength aluminium is susceptible to stress-corrosion cracking in the short-transverse direction under sustained tension. For 7075 specify -T73 or -T76 over -T6 and accept the strength penalty; for 2024 use a -T8xx temper.
ZONE 12

Weighted trade study

Score candidates against criteria you weight yourself. Screening in the selector narrows the field; this ranks what survives.

THIS CONSUMES THE SELECTOR The candidates scored here are whatever passed your filters in the material selector, so set the limits there first. A trade study on an unfiltered database ranks materials you have already ruled out.

Weighted trade study

A single performance index answers one question. Real selection balances several, so set the weights that reflect your actual requirement and score the shortlist. Each criterion is normalised across the candidates currently passing your filters, so the score is relative to the field you are choosing from — not an absolute merit.

Criteria weights

Scoring notes

SCORED AT YOUR DESIGN CONDITIONMass efficiency uses yield derated to the design temperature and adjusted for the selected composite layup; toughness uses the selected orientation and band; fatigue uses the Marin-corrected endurance. Change the service condition in the panel above and the ranking changes with it. Materials above their service ceiling are excluded entirely.
HOW THE SCORE WORKSEach criterion is scaled 0–1 across the current candidate set — log-scaled where the property spans orders of magnitude, so one extreme material cannot swamp the result. Scores are then weighted and summed, and normalised so the best candidate reads 100.
A TRADE STUDY IS AN ARGUMENT, NOT AN ANSWERThe ranking only reflects the weights you chose. Change the weights and the winner changes — which is exactly why the weights, not the score, are the part that needs justifying in a design review. Record them.
READ THE NUMBERS PROPERLY These are typical room-temperature values for common product forms — for first-pass selection only. Stress work needs A/B-basis allowables from MMPDS or the governing AMS/DEF STAN spec, at the right thickness, temper, orientation and temperature. Composite strengths are fibre-direction only. The £/kg* column is an order-of-magnitude indication for comparison, not a quotation — get real prices from your supply chain.
SPECIFIC STRENGTH (UTS ÷ DENSITY) — TOP 18 OF CURRENT FILTER. HIGHER = MORE STRENGTH PER KG
TEMPERATURE CAPABILITY vs COST — THE REAL TRADE. UP = HOTTER, RIGHT = PRICIER

How to read the trade

Bottom-left is where you want to live: cheap and adequate. Every step up the vertical axis tends to cost roughly an order of magnitude along the horizontal one — which is why hot components are built as small inserts inside cooler, cheaper structure rather than machined from one piece of the expensive stuff.

THE INSERT PRINCIPLE A tungsten or carbon-carbon throat insert inside a steel or composite shell costs a fraction of a monolithic refractory nozzle and weighs far less. Same logic as carbide tips brazed to a steel tool body.
£/kg IS NOT £/PART Refractories and superalloys machine slowly and eat tooling, so the machining line on your quote grows with the material price. A part in Inconel 718 can cost 10-20× the same part in 17-4PH once cycle time is counted — see the cost tool.
MATERIAL ρ g/cm³ UTS MPa YIELD MPa σ/ρ MAX °C £/kg* CORR.MACH. SPECS / NOTES
ALUMINIUM TRAPS 7075-T6 is prone to stress-corrosion cracking in the short-transverse direction — use T73 where SCC matters. 2024 and 7075 are effectively non-weldable and pit badly unclad; protect (anodise / Alocrom + primer). 6082 is the UK workhorse: weldable, cheap, everywhere.
STAINLESS & TITANIUM TRAPS 17-4PH condition matters enormously — always state it (e.g. H1025); H900 is strongest but tough on stress corrosion. Ti-6Al-4V galls: never run titanium on titanium without coating, and use anti-seize on Ti threads. 316L work-hardens — rigid setups, sharp tools.
GALVANIC PAIRS Carbon fibre + aluminium, or steel fasteners in bare aluminium, corrode in service. Isolate: Alocrom/anodise, sealant, cadmium- or Zn-Ni-plated fasteners, or sacrificial washers. Check your programme's approved finishes list.
DEFAULT PICKS General bracketry: Al 6082-T6. Flight structure sheet: 2024-T3 clad. High-strength lugs/fittings: 7075-T73 or Ti-6Al-4V. Shafts/gears: EN24T. Corrosive + strong: 17-4PH. Wet systems: 316L. Wear pads/insulators: POM or PEEK.
DESIGN NOTES — DECISIONS, TRAPS AND CHECK SEQUENCES
CONCEPT DOWN-SELECT — IN ONE LINE Agree the weights before scoring, and treat must-haves as pass/fail rather than weighted points.

A down-select is only defensible if someone else could repeat it and reach the same answer.

Procedure

  1. Kill criteria first. Must-have requirements are pass/fail. A concept that fails one is out, however well it scores elsewhere.
  2. Weights before scores. Agree the weights with the team and record them before anyone scores a concept.
  3. Score against evidence. Each score points to a reason — a calculation, a quote, a precedent.
  4. Sensitivity check. Nudge each weight. If one small change flips the winner, the concepts are effectively equal.
  5. Tie-break on risk. Between equal concepts, pick the one with the fewest unknowns.
TRAP Weights adjusted after scoring until the favoured concept wins. It's common, it's usually unconscious, and it's why the weights have to be written down first.
DESIGN RULE Record the rejected concepts and why. When requirements change later — they will — you'll want to know which rejected option the change brings back into play.
⚠ A weighted score is a way of making your priorities explicit and comparing consistently — it is not a decision. The weights are yours, and the ranking is only as defensible as they are.
ZONE 54

Machined-part cost analysis

Rough-order-of-magnitude estimator for CNC parts from billet. It won't replace a quote, but it shows you where the money goes — which is what you need at design time.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

Inputs

Result

£0 / part
Internal corner radius sets the smallest usable cutter, and the cutter sets the cycle time. Aim for R ≥ ⅓ of pocket depth, one common radius throughout, and slightly larger than a stock cutter (R5.2 beats R5 — no dwell mark). A truly sharp internal corner cannot be milled at all.
WHAT ACTUALLY DRIVES MACHINING COST Number of setups (every re-fixture ≈ new datums + time), tightest tolerance on the part, smallest internal corner radius (drives cutter size → time), depth-to-width of pockets, and surface finish below Ra 0.8. One needless ±0.01 can double a part's price.
EASY WINS Internal radii ≥ ⅓ pocket depth and one common radius everywhere. General tolerance per ISO 2768-m and only tighten what mates. Design so one face does everything (single setup). Buy stock near net size. Batch parts to amortise setup — see how the per-part price falls as you raise quantity above.
DESIGN NOTES — DECISIONS, TRAPS AND CHECK SEQUENCES
MACHINING COST — IN ONE LINE Setups dominate one-off cost; cycle time and material dominate production cost — and tight tolerances multiply both.

Design moves that cut cost most

  • Fewer setups — put critical features on faces reachable from one orientation.
  • Internal corner radii of at least a third of pocket depth, so standard cutters reach.
  • Pocket depth under about four times tool diameter.
  • Avoid walls thinner than about 1 mm in aluminium; they chatter.
  • Relax every tolerance that doesn't serve a function.
ZONE 23

Rocket motor components

Component-by-component material selection and how each gets defined on a drawing. Scope is structural and hardware — cases, closures, nozzles, insulation substrates, seals and interfaces. Propellant formulation, grain design and energetics processing sit with your propulsion and energetics specialists and their safety authority.

☛ CLICK ANY NUMBERED COMPONENT to jump to the tool that sizes or selects it. · SCHEMATIC ARRANGEMENT ONLY — not to scale, no design dimensions implied. Each numbered item is covered below.
The three pressures every case design is judged against.

MEOP, proof and burst

  • MEOP — maximum expected operating pressure. Everything is referenced to this, and it must include temperature effects and manufacturing spread, not just the nominal.
  • Proof — applied to every unit (or a defined sample) to demonstrate no yielding or leakage. Typically a modest factor above MEOP.
  • Burst — the demonstrated ultimate capability, shown by analysis and by test to destruction on qualification articles.
THE FACTORS ARE NOT YOURS TO PICK Proof and burst factors come from the governing requirement — DEF STAN 07-085, the programme design rules, or AIAA S-080/S-081 for pressure vessels — not from a textbook or from precedent on a different programme. Confirm them with your stress and safety authority before sizing anything.

Insensitive munitions (IM) & case design

IM design is about making the hardware fail gracefully when something goes wrong — not about performance. The governing policy is STANAG 4439 with AOP-39; each threat has its own test STANAG and a maximum permitted response.

THE CENTRAL IDEA An unplanned stimulus will ignite the propellant. You cannot usually prevent that. What you can design is what happens next: if the case holds pressure, you get an explosion; if the case opens early and stays open, you get a fire. Every IM feature below is a way of guaranteeing the case opens before it can burst. That is why IM work is a case, closure and venting problem as much as a formulation problem.

Threats and required responses

THREATSTANDARDWHAT IT SIMULATESMAX RESPONSEDESIGN IMPLICATION

AOP-39 response descriptors

TYPERESPONSEWHAT IT MEANS
READ THE DIRECTION Type I is the worst, Type VI the best — the numbering runs opposite to how people instinctively read it. "Type V or better" means burning, deflagration is already a fail for most threats.

Mitigation features

SLOW COOK-OFF IS THE HARD CASE Fast heating tends to look after itself on a composite motor — the resin softens and the case relieves early. Slow heating brings the whole item up together, so the propellant can reach reaction temperature while the case is still cold-strong and fully intact. Most deliberate venting features exist because of slow cook-off, not fast.

Heritage → modern material lineage

What propulsion hardware used to be made from, what it is made from now, and — more usefully — why it changed. In most cases the driver was manufacturing process, not a better alloy.

THE PATTERN WORTH NOTICING Across almost every line above, the change was driven by how the part is made rather than by a stronger material. Additive manufacturing let designers put cooling channels inside a liner instead of brazing them on, and print refractories that were previously near-impossible to form. When you are selecting a material, ask what process it enables — that is usually where the real gain is.

Material selection & motor performance

Every material choice on a motor lands on one of a handful of performance factors. This maps the class of material to what it actually buys and costs you at motor level, rather than at coupon level.

THE ONE NUMBER THAT MATTERS Propellant mass fraction — propellant mass over total motor mass — dominates delivered performance. Every gram of case, insulation, nozzle and hardware is a gram of propellant you are not carrying. That is why case material choice is the single largest performance lever available to a hardware designer, and why insulation thickness is never "just a bit more to be safe".
PERIPHERAL COARSE GRAIN — A MANUFACTURING RESTRICTION WITH PERFORMANCE CONSEQUENCES Where PCG is prohibited, the minimum stock removal is not free: it sets the minimum purchased section, adds machining time, and can force a heavier starting billet or plate. Establish the requirement before sizing the part, or you will find the finished wall thickness no longer closes after the skin comes off.
DESIGN ORDER THAT WORKS Fix MEOP and the proof/burst factors first, then choose the case material class, then size the wall, then add insulation, then check what mass fraction you actually have left. Choosing the material last — after the geometry is frozen — is how motors end up overweight with no options remaining.

Grain configurations & thrust profile

Grain geometry sets the burning surface area as the web regresses, and burning surface sets the thrust-time trace. As a hardware designer you inherit this: it dictates insulation profile, stress-relief features and where the bondline is loaded.

CONFIGURATIONBURN PROFILEGEOMETRYDESIGN CONSEQUENCE
THE THREE PROFILES Progressive — burning surface grows, pressure and thrust rise. Neutral — surface roughly constant, flat trace. Regressive — surface shrinks, thrust falls away. Most motors aim for neutral so the case sees one steady design pressure rather than a climbing one.

Motor design factors & their tensions

Every one of these is a trade, not a target. The second column is what it buys you; the third is what it costs you — which is where the design work actually happens.

⚠ Descriptive engineering reference. Motor ballistic design, propellant selection, IM qualification and all energetics work are governed by JSP 520, DEF STAN 07-085 and your programme safety case, and remain the responsibility of the appropriate qualified specialists and safety authority.

Defining rocket motor hardware on a drawing

MATERIAL BLOCK — SAY MORE THAN THE ALLOY The alloy name alone is not a specification. State: alloy + condition/temper + product form + governing spec + melt practice where it matters. "D6AC BAR PER AMS 6431, VAR, HT TO 1520 MPa MIN UTS, DOUBLE TEMPER" is a specification; "D6AC" is a wish.
SPECIAL PROCESSES NEED THEIR OWN CALLOUTS Heat treatment (with AMS 2750 pyrometry), welding procedure, NDT method + acceptance class, coating, and cleanliness are each separate notes with a separate spec. If it can't be verified by measuring the finished part, it needs an approved process and a certificate.
FRACTURE-CRITICAL PARTS CHANGE THE RULES Once a part is classified fracture-critical, the drawing must carry the flaw-size and NDE requirements that go with it, and material comes from a controlled quality class (ultrasonic grade, melt practice). Get the classification agreed before you finalise tolerances — it drives surface finish, radii and inspection access.
TRACEABILITY IS A DRAWING REQUIREMENT Batch/heat number marking, cert retention, and the marking method (etch vs stamp — stamping is a stress raiser and is banned on many fracture-critical surfaces) all belong on the sheet. State the marking location and method explicitly.

Interfaces that bite

DISSIMILAR METALS Case steel to aluminium closure, or carbon composite to any metal, sets up a galvanic cell that will find every gap in your protective scheme. Specify isolation (sealant, primer, isolating film) and a bonding/earthing path deliberately — they pull in opposite directions.
DIFFERENTIAL THERMAL EXPANSION A refractory insert in a steel or composite housing sees large temperature swings across a joint between materials with very different expansion coefficients. Interference at room temperature and gap at temperature (or the reverse) is a design decision — state the assembly temperature on the drawing when the fit depends on it.
SEALS IN HOT / ENERGETIC ENVIRONMENTS Standard NBR and even FKM assumptions do not carry over. Confirm compatibility with the actual fluids and temperature profile, and check whether your programme mandates specific approved seal materials — many do. Where a seal is safety-significant, its groove tolerances get the same scrutiny as structure.
BONDLINES ARE STRUCTURE Insulation-to-case and liner bonds carry load and are the usual failure path. Define surface preparation, adhesive spec, bondline thickness, cure schedule and the NDT method for verifying the bond — a bond with no inspection requirement is an unverified joint.
⚠ This page is a design-office aide-mémoire for structural hardware. It is not a substitute for DEF STAN 07-085, JSP 520, your programme's design rules manual, or your safety authority. Anything touching energetics, initiation, or motor performance goes through the responsible specialists.
ZONE 24

Solid propellant families & materials compatibility

What the main solid propellant classes are, how they behave as engineering materials, and — the part that actually lands on your drawings — which materials are allowed anywhere near them.

SCOPE OF THIS PAGE This is a descriptive and compatibility reference for hardware designers. It deliberately contains no formulations, proportions, processing parameters, burn-rate tailoring or grain design — those sit with your energetics and propulsion specialists under JSP 520 and your programme safety authority, and nothing here substitutes for their approval. What it does cover is the design-office question: what is this stuff like to build hardware around, and what can touch it.

Propellant families

Materials compatibility

COMPATIBILITY IS PROPELLANT-SPECIFIC — THIS IS THE KEY POINT A material is not "compatible with propellant" in the abstract. Nitrate-ester systems and composite systems degrade by entirely different mechanisms, so the same metal can be prohibited against one and merely controlled against the other. Nine of the sixteen materials below change verdict between families. Read across the row, not down a single column.

How compatibility is actually established

Compatibility is demonstrated by test, not asserted from a datasheet. STANAG 4147 is the governing agreement for chemical compatibility of ammunition components with explosives and propellants; the methods below are its principal tools.

METHODWHAT IT MEASURESAPPLICABILITY
WHY THE TEST LIST ITSELF PROVES THE POINT Stabiliser depletion only means something for a nitrocellulose-based propellant — a composite has no stabiliser to deplete. The fact that the standard's methods differ by propellant family is the clearest possible evidence that the compatibility verdicts must too.
THE COPPER RULE If you remember one thing from this page: copper and copper alloys are excluded around nitrate-ester (double-base) propellant. That means no brass fittings, no bronze bushes, no beryllium copper tools, no copper-bearing solder, and no copper plating — in the hardware, the tooling, the handling equipment or the storage area. It is easy to violate accidentally through a bought-in component.
THE SILICONE RULE Silicone is banned from most propellant and bond areas — not for reactivity, but because it migrates, transfers on contact and destroys adhesive bonds. Since case-to-insulation and insulation-to-propellant bonds are structural, a silicone fingerprint can fail a motor. This extends to release agents, sealants, lubricants and hand creams.
COMPATIBILITY IS TESTED, NOT ASSUMED Formal compatibility assessment normally involves accelerated ageing of the material in contact with the propellant and measuring the effect on both. A material being "chemically inert" on a datasheet proves nothing about a specific pairing over a decades-long service life. Ask for the compatibility evidence before you specify.
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR DRAWINGS Contact materials, finishes, seals, adhesives and even temporary protective materials all need to come from the approved list. State them explicitly and never leave a finish or a seal material to shop discretion on hardware that sees propellant.
⚠ Descriptive reference only. Anything involving energetic materials — selection, processing, handling, storage, disposal or test — is governed by JSP 520, DEF STAN 07-085 and your programme safety case, and is the responsibility of the appropriate qualified specialists and safety authority.
ZONE 58

Material specification builder

Pick a material and get everything you need to write the material block: which standard governs each product form (bar, plate, tube, forging), the available tempers and heat treatments, the finishes you can call up, a copy-ready drawing callout, and the practical tips that stop it going wrong.

Stock forms

What you are actually buying. A section says more than a name — and the form decides grain direction, tolerance class and how much of it you machine away.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THE THREE-PART RULE A complete metal callout needs three things, and most drawings only carry one or two: (1) the alloy and condition, (2) the product form standard — because properties and tolerances differ between bar, plate and extrusion — and (3) the finish with its own spec. "6082-T6" is a hope. "EN AW-6082-T6 EXTRUDED BAR TO BS EN 755-2, TOLERANCES TO BS EN 755-3" is a specification.
ZONE 16

Metal designation cross-reference

The same alloy has a different name in every system you'll meet. This maps the common name to its BS EN / ISO designation, EN material number, the legacy British spec still on heritage drawings, the UNS number, and the aerospace spec you'd actually procure to.

BS L-series aerospace specifications

What a UK aerospace drawing actually calls up — —. An alloy name is not a callout: the spec fixes form, temper and tolerance as well as chemistry.

TWO SPECS CAN BE THE SAME METAL AND STILL NOT INTERCHANGEABLE L164 and L166 are both 2014A clad sheet in T4, with identical chemistry and mechanical requirements. L166 is held to tighter rolling tolerance. Stock is often dual-certified to both — but a drawing calling L166 is not satisfied by material certified only to L164.
WHICH ONE GOES ON THE DRAWING? In the UK, working to BS 8888, the BS EN designation plus the governing product standard is the correct call-out — e.g. EN AW-6082-T6 TO BS EN 755-2. Add the UNS or AMS number in brackets only where the supply chain genuinely needs it. Legacy BS specs (HE30, 817M40, 304S11) are for reading old drawings, not for writing new ones.
EQUIVALENT IS NOT IDENTICAL Cross-reference tables map nearest grades, not interchangeable ones. Composition ranges, permitted impurities, melt practice, test requirements and acceptance criteria differ between systems. Never substitute across a row on a flight or safety-significant part without engineering approval and a materials review — and be especially careful where the aerospace spec (AMS, AIR) carries melt-practice and cleanliness requirements the commercial EN grade does not.
COMMON NAMEBS EN / ISO DESIGNATIONEN No. LEGACY BSUNSAERO / OTHER SPECNOTE

How to read the numbering systems

EN ALUMINIUM — EN 573 EN AW-6082: AW = aluminium wrought (AC = cast). The four digits match the international 6xxx system. Chemical composition is EN 573-3; you also need the product standard for properties — EN 485 sheet/plate, EN 755 extrusion, EN 754 drawn bar/tube.
EN STEEL — EN 10027 Two parallel systems. Names (34CrNiMo6) encode composition: carbon ×100, then alloying elements with factored percentages. Numbers (1.6582) are just catalogue entries — 1.0xxx–1.9xxx steels, 2.xxxx non-ferrous heavy metals, 3.xxxx light metals.
EN STAINLESS — EN 10088 X2CrNiMo17-12-2 = X (high alloy), carbon ×100, elements, then percentages. That is 316L, number 1.4404. Part 2 is sheet/plate, Part 3 is bar/rod/section.
UNS A single letter plus five digits, covering everything: A = aluminium, S = stainless, N = nickel, R = reactive/refractory (titanium), G = carbon/alloy steel, C = copper, K = misc steels. Often the cleanest way to pin down exactly which grade someone means.
ZONE 17

Density register

Every material likely to appear on a rocket programme or in its tooling — metals, alloys, polymers, glass, ceramics, composites, cores, woods and workshop materials. Primary column is kg/mm³ as requested; g/cm³ and kg/m³ sit alongside for sanity checking.

UNITS — READ THIS ONCE kg/mm³ produces very small numbers: steel is 0.00000785 kg/mm³. The conversion is simply g/cm³ ÷ 1,000,000. Values here are shown in full decimal to 9 places — count the zeros carefully. If you are entering density into FEA using the mm / N / tonne consistent unit system (Abaqus, LS-DYNA, most mm-based solvers), the value it wants is tonne/mm³ = 0.00000000785 for steel — that is your kg/mm³ figure × 10⁻³. Mixing the two is the single most common cause of a model coming out 1000× too heavy.
MATERIAL CATEGORY kg/mm³ g/cm³ kg/m³ TYPICAL USE

ZONE 18

Plastics reference

What the acronym means, what it is sold as, what it is good for, and — more usefully — what it is bad at. Sorted from commodity through to the high-performance polymers.

Acronym quick-lookup

ACRONYMFULL NAMEALSO SOLD ASMIN °CMAX °CTg °CH₂O %µOUTGAS
THE COLD END KILLS MORE SEALS THAN THE HOT END Datasheets lead with maximum temperature, but a polymer below its glass transition is a different material — hard, brittle and with almost no elastic recovery. A seal that is fine at 200 °C can leak on a cold morning. Standard FKM stiffens around −20 °C, which is why low-temperature grades exist; silicone and PTFE stay useful far colder than almost anything else.
VACUUM OUTGASSING For anything flying or in a vacuum chamber, outgassing matters as much as strength — volatiles condense on optics, sensors and cold surfaces. The screening standard is ASTM E595 with limits of TML < 1.0% and CVCM < 0.10%. The ratings here are indicative: verify the specific compound and cure against the NASA outgassing database, because fillers, plasticisers and cure state change the result far more than the base polymer does.
WATER ABSORPTION MOVES DIMENSIONS Nylon absorbs up to about 1.8% and grows accordingly — which is why PA is a poor choice for precision parts and POM or PET is preferred. Absorbed moisture also plasticises the polymer, dropping stiffness and strength while raising toughness.
RADIATION PTFE and the perfluoropolymers are the outlier here: superb chemically, but among the worst materials under ionising radiation, degrading at doses other polymers shrug off. PEEK, PEI, PI and PPS are the radiation-tolerant choices.
TEMPERATURES ARE CONTINUOUS-SERVICE GUIDES Short excursions can go higher; sustained load at temperature must go lower. Any polymer under continuous stress creeps, and the creep rate climbs steeply as you approach these figures — check creep data, not just the temperature rating, before you load a plastic part in service.
ZONE 47

Thread reference — all systems

Every thread system you'll meet on UK aerospace & defence work: metric first, then Unified, Whitworth, BA and the pipe families. Dimensions, tap and clearance drills, tolerance classes, where each system belongs — and the cross-system traps that wreck hardware.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THE GOLDEN CROSS-SYSTEM RULES 1/4-20 UNC and 1/4 BSW share diameter and TPI but not form angle (60° vs 55°) — they part-assemble then strip. 1/2 UNC is 13 TPI, 1/2 BSW is 12. NPT and BSPT look alike and leak forever when mixed. M10×1.5 and M10×1.25 differ by a quarter-millimetre of pitch. The rule: identify by gauging, never by eye, and state the full designation with pitch/TPI on every callout.

System guides

THREAD ENGAGEMENT — THE COLOURED COLUMN Engagement is computed as (major − drill) ÷ (1.299 × pitch) for 60° forms, and ÷ (1.2806 × pitch) for the 55° Whitworth form. Green 60–80% is the sensible working band. Note the traditional Whitworth tapping drills run tighter (80–85%) than modern metric practice — that is genuinely how the published BSW/BSF tables are, not an error. Open them up slightly in tough materials.
TAP DRILL LOGIC Metric rule: tap drill = nominal − pitch, giving ~77% thread engagement. Engagement above ~75% adds torque and broken taps, not strength — the joint fails by bolt fracture or thread shear long before percentage matters. In tough materials (stainless, Inconel, titanium) drop to ~65%: drill fractionally larger than D−P.
CLEARANCE HOLE LOGIC ISO 273 gives close (H12), medium (H13) and coarse (H14) series. Medium is the default; close only where the fastener locates the part (better: don't — use dowels); coarse for painted, galvanised or multi-part stacks where tolerances accumulate.
WHICH SYSTEM FOR NEW DESIGN Metric coarse, tolerance 6H/6g, full stop — unless the interface forces otherwise: US-origin equipment (Unified, class 2A/2B or 3A/3B), fluid ports (G with face seal), or legacy repair (match the original). Never introduce a new Whitworth or BA thread.
AEROSPACE EXTERNALS Fatigue-critical external threads on US-influenced programmes are UNJ form to AS8879 — enlarged, controlled root radius, rolled after heat treatment. The equivalent metric MJ form is ISO 5855. A standard cut 6g thread is not a substitute where the stress report assumed rolled UNJ/MJ.
DESIGN NOTES — DECISIONS, TRAPS AND CHECK SEQUENCES
THREADS & INSERTS — IN ONE LINE The bolt must yield before the thread strips — a yielded bolt shows itself, a stripped thread doesn't.

Minimum engagement

Tapped materialEngagementNotes
Steel into steel, similar strength1.0 × dStandard nut height is sized on this
Steel into titanium1.2–1.5 × dGalling risk — lubricate
Steel into aluminium1.5–2.0 × dUse 2× if cycled
Steel into magnesium2.5–3.0 × dInsert strongly preferred

These are rules of thumb. Calculate stripping strength for critical joints — VDI 2230 covers it.

MJ threads for fatigue-critical joints

Aerospace MJ threads (ISO 5855) have a controlled, larger root radius and modified tolerances. The root is where fatigue cracks start, so the radius matters more than any other thread detail. Pair with rolled after heat treatment — the compressive residual stress in the root greatly improves fatigue life over cut threads. Write the phrase in full on the drawing; “rolled thread” alone doesn't guarantee the sequence.

When to use an insert

  • More than a handful of assembly cycles into aluminium.
  • Blind tapped holes in expensive parts.
  • Anywhere a stripped thread would mean a scrapped flight part.

Wire inserts improve load share across engaged threads. Keyed solid inserts resist vibration and torque-out better.

Galling

Titanium and austenitic stainless gall against themselves and each other. Avoid same-alloy pairs, use silver-plated nuts or dry film lubricant, and record the effect of the lubricant on torque.

TRAP Never let a thread run-out, tapped hole or cross-drilling break into a sealing surface or fillet. It creates a leak path that's usually found at proof test.

O-ring design calculator

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

ON THE STANDARD The O-ring standard is BS ISO 3601: Part 1 gives inside diameters, cross-sections and tolerances; Part 2 gives the housing (gland) dimensions; Part 3 quality acceptance; Part 4 anti-extrusion (back-up) rings; Part 5 material suitability. (BS 3601 on its own is the carbon steel pipe and tube standard — different thing entirely, easy to mistype.)

Inputs

Recommended seal & groove

—

Groove geometry

Material selector

Materials are checked live against the temperature and media you entered above. Green = suitable, amber = limited or check the specific grade, red = do not use.

CODEMATERIALTEMP RANGEFITNOTES & WATCH-OUTS

Media compatibility matrix

SURFACE FINISH Groove and counterface finish matters as much as the dimensions. Typical guidance: static Ra 1.6 max on sealing surfaces, dynamic Ra 0.4 max on the sliding counterface, and Ra 3.2 on non-sealing groove walls. Too rough leaks; too smooth (below about Ra 0.1) can starve a dynamic seal of lubricant.
LEAD-IN CHAMFERS Every edge the O-ring passes over on assembly needs a 15–20° lead-in chamfer, deburred and blended. More O-rings are killed during assembly than in service — a sharp bore edge or an unbroken cross-hole will shave the ring and you will never see it once assembled.
GROOVE CORNER RADII Keep bottom corners small (roughly 0.1–0.3 mm depending on cross-section) so the ring seats properly, but never leave them sharp — a sharp corner is a stress raiser in the ring and a crack initiator in the metal.
WHAT THIS TOOL IS NOT A first-pass sizing aid using the ISO 3601-2 target bands. It does not replace the standard, the seal manufacturer's catalogue, or a compatibility test with your actual fluid at your actual temperature. Confirm the final size and tolerances against ISO 3601-1 before release.
DESIGN NOTES — DECISIONS, TRAPS AND CHECK SEQUENCES
O-RING DESIGN — IN ONE LINE Check squeeze at the worst tolerance corner and the coldest temperature, with the joint gap at its widest under pressure.

Design the squeeze, then let the groove follow. Every seal works at nominal — the design is judged at the corners.

Target squeeze and fill

DutySqueezeGland fill
Static face seal20–30%75–85%
Static radial seal15–25%75–85%
Reciprocating dynamic10–18%70–80%

Extrusion limits pressure

The seal fails by being forced into the clearance gap. Screening values below are diametral clearance (radial gap is half). Use the supplier's chart for design.

Pressure70 Shore A90 Shore A
< 5 MPa≤ 0.15 mm≤ 0.25 mm
5–10 MPa≤ 0.08 mm≤ 0.15 mm
> 10 MPabackup ring≤ 0.08 mm or backup ring

Use the widest gap in service: maximum clearance, at maximum temperature, with the bore dilated under pressure. Checking only the cold assembly gap misses the case that fails.

The joint moves — the seal must follow

Under pressure, a joint opens slightly: flanges lift, bores dilate, mating parts rotate. An elastomer seal only keeps sealing if it springs back fast enough to follow that movement.

LESSON The 1986 Challenger loss traced to a joint whose gap opened under pressure while its O-rings were too cold to follow it. Two checks apply to any pressure joint: how far the gap opens under load, and whether the seal can track it at minimum temperature.

Cold is the dangerous end

Near its glass transition an elastomer stops behaving like a spring. Below TR-10, sealing relies almost entirely on squeeze built into the metal. Specify the compound by low-temperature capability and check squeeze with both parts contracted.

Other checks

  • Compression set — budget permanent loss into minimum squeeze, especially after long storage.
  • Thermal swell — elastomer expansion is many times the metal's. Check gland fill hot, at minimum groove volume. Over ~90% risks hydraulic lock.
  • Finish — Ra 0.8 static, Ra 0.4 dynamic; machining lay must not cross the seal.
  • Lead-in — 15–20° chamfer, deburred, or the seal is cut on assembly unseen.
ELASTOMER COMPOUNDS — IN ONE LINE Pick the compound for the coldest, hottest and chemically worst moment — in that order.

Elastomer families cover broad ranges and individual compounds vary widely within them. Use this to shortlist, then select a specific compound from a supplier with data for your fluid and temperature.

TRAP Assembly lubricant. An EPDM seal greased with a petroleum-based lubricant swells and fails, even though the service fluid is compatible. Specify the assembly lubricant on the drawing alongside the compound.

Other checks

  • Low temperature — use TR-10, not the brittle point. Brittle point is far colder than where sealing performance is lost.
  • Shelf life — record cure date; age-control and storage conditions follow your company's spec.
  • Compression set — at temperature and time, not just the datasheet's standard condition.
  • Explosive decompression — for gas service with rapid depressurisation, use an ED-rated compound.

ISO 286 limits & fits

Enter a size and a tolerance class, get the actual limits in millimetres, the resulting clearance or interference, and what kind of fit you have actually specified.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

HOLE BASIS IS THE DEFAULT Keep the hole at H and vary the shaft letter. The hole is made by a tool of fixed size — drill, reamer, broach — so it is far cheaper to hold the hole constant and grind the shaft to suit. Shaft basis (shaft at h) is for drawn bar and shafting used as-supplied, or where one shaft carries several different fits along its length.

Inputs

Tolerance zones

IT grades at this size

WHAT THE GRADE MEANS IN PRACTICE IT01–IT4 gauge and instrument work · IT5–IT7 fits and bearing seats · IT8–IT9 general machining · IT10–IT11 sheet, castings and clearance holes · IT12–IT16 as-cast, as-forged and flame-cut. Every grade tighter roughly doubles the cost of the feature — do not specify H6 where H9 works.

ISO 2768 general tolerances

The tolerance that applies to every dimension you did not tolerance individually. Part 1 covers linear and angular dimensions, Part 2 covers geometry. In the UK these are adopted as BS EN 22768-1 and -2.

CHECK WHICH STANDARD YOUR PROGRAMME USES ISO 2768-2 has been superseded by ISO 22081, which replaces the fixed H/K/L geometry classes with a general geometrical specification referenced to stated datums. Many organisations still work to 2768 and plenty of legacy drawings carry it, so both are in circulation — confirm which applies before you put it in a title block.

WHAT IT DOES NOT COVER ISO 2768 says nothing about roundness or cylindricity — those are limited by the size tolerance. Parallelism is not tabulated either: it takes the larger of the size tolerance and the flatness/straightness value. Anything functionally important still needs its own explicit tolerance.
IT IS NOT A LICENCE TO STOP TOLERANCING A general tolerance covers the dimensions that genuinely do not matter. If a feature locates something, seals, or carries load, tolerance it individually — and remember that a general tolerance still has to be achievable and inspectable on every dimension it silently applies to.
THE USUAL CALL-OUT ISO 2768-mK is the common general-purpose pairing: medium linear with class K geometry. Write it in the title block, not buried in a note, and make sure the class you pick matches the process — specifying -f on a sand casting is meaningless.
BROKEN EDGES External radii and chamfer heights get their own, much looser table — typically ±0.2 mm up to 3 mm for classes f and m. Do not assume the linear tolerance applies to an edge break.

INTERFERENCE FITS NEED MORE THAN LIMITS A press fit also needs assembly force, hoop stress in the outer part, and the temperature differential if you intend to shrink it on. Check the fit is still adequate at maximum service temperature — a shrink fit that relaxes when hot has no retention at all.

Temperature

A fit is chosen at 20°C but has to work at the extremes. An aluminium housing on a steel shaft gains clearance hot and loses it cold. Recalculate the fit at both ends — see Differential expansion.

ZONE 48

Bolted joint & torque calculator

Preload, tightening torque, stress area and thread engagement for metric fasteners — with the friction sensitivity shown, because friction is what actually decides whether your torque produces the preload you wanted.

TORQUE IS A POOR PROXY FOR PRELOAD — READ THIS FIRST Roughly 85–90% of applied torque is consumed by friction under the head and in the threads. Only the remainder stretches the bolt. A change in friction coefficient from 0.10 to 0.16 — entirely plausible between a lubricated and an as-received fastener — changes the achieved preload by around 40% for the same torque. Published torque tables disagree with each other by 10–15% for exactly this reason. This tool follows the VDI 2230 convention — 90% of Rp0.2 reduced for tightening torsion, with Dkm = 1.36·d — and reproduces published VDI values within about 10%. Treat any torque figure, including this one, as a starting point subject to your own joint analysis.

Inputs

Result

—

Friction sensitivity

The same torque across the range of plausible friction conditions. The spread is the reason torque-controlled tightening has such poor preload accuracy.

CONDITIONµTORQUE FOR TARGET PRELOADPRELOAD AT FIXED TORQUEvs TARGET

Where the torque goes

BETTER THAN TORQUE Angle-controlled (torque-to-yield) tightening, bolt elongation measurement, ultrasonic length measurement, or load-indicating washers all give far better preload accuracy than a torque wrench. If the joint matters, control something closer to preload than torque.
ENGAGEMENT AND STRIPPING The engagement figures here are the usual rules of thumb. A proper check compares the thread shear area of the internal and external threads so the bolt fails in tension before the tapped thread strips — a bolt failure is detectable, a stripped thread often is not.
HYDROGEN EMBRITTLEMENT Class 10.9 and 12.9 fasteners are susceptible after electroplating. Specify the relief bake to BS EN ISO 4042, with the time limit after plating, or use mechanically plated or non-electroplated finishes.
STAINLESS GALLS A2 and A4 fasteners seize on assembly with alarming regularity, especially in coarse threads and at speed. Specify an anti-seize or dry film lubricant, and note that doing so changes the friction and therefore the torque.
DESIGN NOTES — DECISIONS, TRAPS AND CHECK SEQUENCES
BOLTED JOINTS — IN ONE LINE Size the joint on minimum preload after losses — the question is whether the joint opens, not whether the bolt breaks.

Dividing external load by bolt area is the wrong calculation for a preloaded joint, and it's wrong in the unsafe direction for a sealed one.

Where external load actually goes

The clamped parts are usually several times stiffer than the bolt, so most applied tension unloads the clamped parts rather than adding to the bolt.

ΔF_bolt = Φ · F_ext Φ = n · K_b / (K_b + K_c) n = load introduction factor (VDI 2230), typically 0.3–0.7 metal-to-metal joints: Φ often ≈ 0.05–0.25

Preload governs, not bolt area. Upsizing the bolt in the same flange stiffens the bolt and raises Φ — it can make fatigue worse.

Tightening factor αA

αA = F_max / F_min for the method. Design separation on F_min; check bolt strength on F_max.

MethodαA≈ scatter
Ultrasonic elongation measurement1.1–1.2±5–9%
Yield-controlled tightening1.2–1.4±9–17%
Angle-controlled tightening1.2–1.4±9–17%
Hydraulic tensioning1.2–1.6±9–23%
Torque, friction found by test on the joint1.4–1.6±17–23%
Torque, friction estimated1.6–2.5±23–43%
Impact wrench2.5–4never structural
TRAP About 90% of applied torque goes into friction under the head and in the threads. A torque value with no stated friction coefficient and lubricant is not an instruction. Put μ and the lubricant in the drawing note.

Losses before checking separation

  • Embedment — surface asperities flatten in the first hours. Use VDI 2230's values by roughness and number of interfaces; a few microns per interface is typical. Short grips lose a much higher percentage of preload.
  • Thermal differential — see below and Thermal growth.
  • Coating or gasket creep — soft platings and gaskets in the clamp stack dominate everything else.
aim for grip ratio l / d ≥ 3 — a long thin bolt is a forgiving spring

Thermal effect on preload

  • Aluminium flange, steel bolt, heating — flange grows more, preload rises. Check the bolt against yield hot.
  • Steel flange, titanium bolt, heating — preload falls. Check separation hot.

Self-loosening

Transverse slip of the clamped parts rotates the nut loose — this is the dominant loosening mechanism, not axial vibration. The real defence is enough clamp force that friction at the interface exceeds transverse load with margin, so the joint never slips. Locking features are a second line, covered in Locking & retention.

Shear joints

Decide whether the joint carries shear by friction (slip-critical — preload and interface friction carry it) or bearing (bolt shank bears on hole walls). Mixing the two in one analysis is a common error. If position must hold after slip, use dowels or a spigot.

Check sequence

  1. Minimum preload after all losses, at the worst temperature.
  2. Separation: remaining clamp exceeds (1 − Φ) · F_ext with margin. For a sealed joint, keep the seal's contact stress — stricter than open-gap.
  3. Slip: clamp × friction × interfaces exceeds transverse load with margin.
  4. Bolt stress at maximum preload plus external plus thermal.
  5. Thread stripping and bearing under the head.
  6. Fatigue on the alternating component, which Φ has already made small. If it isn't small, the joint is under-preloaded.
ZONE 52

Galvanic corrosion & dissimilar metals

Aerospace hardware mixes aluminium, titanium, steel, stainless and carbon composite in the same joint. Pick any two and find out whether that joint will survive, which part corrodes, and what to do about it.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THE THREE THINGS A GALVANIC CELL NEEDS Two materials of different potential, an electrical connection between them, and an electrolyte bridging them. Remove any one and there is no corrosion. That is the whole basis of every mitigation below — you either move the materials closer in potential, break the electrical path, or keep the water out.

The couple

AREA RATIO IS THE MULTIPLIER EVERYONE FORGETS A large cathode driving a small anode concentrates all the attack into a tiny area. A steel fastener in an aluminium panel is survivable; an aluminium fastener in a steel or carbon panel is eaten. Get the small part on the cathodic (noble) side.

Verdict

—

Mitigation

Galvanic series

Anodic index in volts. Higher is more anodic and corrodes preferentially; lower is more noble and drives the attack. The two selected materials are highlighted.

INDEX VMATERIALBEHAVIOURΔV TO SELECTION 1
CARBON COMPOSITE IS NOT INERT Carbon fibre is almost as noble as gold, so a CFRP-to-aluminium joint is one of the most aggressive couples in normal engineering — roughly 0.80 V. It is a genuine and frequent cause of structural corrosion. Always isolate: a glass-fibre ply on the bond face, a sealant layer, or a titanium or stainless interface fitting.
WHY CADMIUM WAS EVERYWHERE Cadmium plating sits almost exactly alongside aluminium in the series, so a cadmium-plated steel fastener in aluminium structure is galvanically near-neutral. That is precisely why aerospace used it for decades. It is being eliminated for toxicity, and the modern replacement — zinc-nickel — is chosen to sit in a similar place.
PASSIVE FILMS DO THE WORK Stainless and titanium behave nobly only while passive. In a crevice starved of oxygen the film cannot repair and the potential shifts markedly more active, so a joint that looks fine on this chart can still corrode in the crevice under a washer or in a faying surface. Design the joint to drain and to be sealed.
THIS IS A SCREENING TOOL Anodic indices are nominal values for the MIL-STD-889 approach. Real behaviour depends on alloy, temper, surface condition, electrolyte chemistry, temperature and crevice geometry. Use it to spot problems early — then confirm against your programme's dissimilar-metals standard.
DESIGN NOTES — DECISIONS, TRAPS AND CHECK SEQUENCES
GALVANIC COMPATIBILITY — IN ONE LINE Galvanic corrosion needs dissimilar metals, an electrolyte and contact — remove any one of the three.

Anodic index (approximate)

Voltage difference between two metals indicates galvanic risk. Values are approximate — verify against MIL-STD-889 for your exact alloys.

MetalIndex V
Gold, platinum0.00
Graphite, CFRP≈0.25
Nickel, titanium, Monel0.30
Copper0.35
Stainless steel, 18% Cr0.50
Stainless steel, 12% Cr0.60
Wrought aluminium, 2000 series0.75
Carbon and low-alloy steel0.85
Wrought aluminium, other series0.90
Cadmium0.95
Zinc1.25
Magnesium1.75
EnvironmentMax difference
Harsh — salt spray, humidity, outdoor0.15 V
Normal — sheltered, no condensation control0.25 V
Controlled — temperature and humidity controlled0.50 V

Area ratio

Small anode, large cathode is the dangerous combination. An aluminium rivet in a stainless sheet corrodes rapidly; a stainless fastener in an aluminium sheet is far more tolerable.

TRAP Carbon fibre is strongly cathodic. Aluminium fastened directly to CFRP corrodes fast. Use titanium fasteners and a glass-ply or sealant isolation layer.

Mitigation, in order of effectiveness

  1. Choose compatible metals.
  2. Isolate them electrically — washers, sleeves, a barrier ply.
  3. Exclude the electrolyte — wet-install fasteners with sealant or primer.
  4. Coat the cathode as well as the anode. Coating only the anode concentrates attack at any scratch.

Motor case & pressure vessel sizing

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

COMPOSITE CASES USE THE LAYUP YOU SELECTED IN THE MATERIAL SELECTOR Composite strength here is the layup-adjusted value, not the unidirectional datasheet figure. A filament-wound case should use the filament wound layup; leaving it on unidirectional will size the case roughly 40% too thin. Metals are unaffected.
THIS TOOL CONSUMES THE REST OF THE SITE Yield is derated to the design temperature using the retention curves, fracture toughness comes from the min/typ/max range at the orientation you selected, and the fatigue check uses the Marin-corrected endurance limit. Inputs

Required wall

—

Pressure schedule

Material comparison at this duty

The same vessel in every material that can carry it — ranked by case mass, which is what actually drives propellant mass fraction.

MEOP IS NOT THE NOMINAL BALLISTIC PRESSURE MEOP must already include grain temperature sensitivity, manufacturing spread in burn rate and web, and any erosive-burning or ignition spike. Sizing a case on the nominal chamber pressure and then discovering the hot-day value is 15% higher is a classic and expensive mistake.
MEMBRANE STRESS IS THE EASY PART This tool gives you the membrane wall. It does not size the domes, the closure joints, the boss or skirt attachments, or anything with a discontinuity — and those are where cases actually fail. Bending at a dome-to-cylinder junction can double the local stress. Treat this as the starting thickness, not the answer.
THIN VS THICK WALL Below about t/r = 0.1 the thin-wall (Barlow) result is within a few percent of the Lamé solution. Above that it becomes unconservative — the tool computes both and tells you which applies.
LEAK BEFORE BURST The critical flaw size tells you whether a crack will grow through the wall and vent, or run unstably. If the critical flaw is smaller than the wall thickness, the vessel can fail catastrophically without leaking first — and your NDT must reliably find flaws well below that size.

Joint separation — the question preload was only half of

MOST OF AN EXTERNAL LOAD DOES NOT REACH THE BOLT A preloaded joint is two springs in parallel. When pressure pulls the closure, the bolt stretches a little more — but the clamped parts unload by much more. Only the fraction Φ reaches the bolt, and Φ is typically 0.15 to 0.35. Sizing a closure bolt for the full separating force overstates the load by three to six times.

FEA & structural test methods

Choosing the right analysis for a motor component, the traps that make a plausible-looking result wrong, and how each physical test correlates back to the model.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THE ONLY QUESTION THAT MATTERS Not “what is the stress?” but “what is the failure mode, and does my analysis capture it?” A linear static run on a buckling-critical skirt gives a comfortable stress and a completely wrong answer. Pick the analysis from the failure mode, not from what is convenient to set up.

Analysis types

Motor component → analysis map

COMPONENTGOVERNING FAILURE MODEANALYSIS REQUIRED

Three material classes, three different analyses

THE CATEGORY ERROR A motor contains a metal case at 200 GPa bonded to a propellant grain at 5 MPa — a stiffness ratio of about 40,000. They are not the same analysis with different numbers in it. They need different constitutive models, different elements, and different failure criteria. Treating a grain like a metal is the most common serious mistake in motor structural analysis.
ASPECTSTRUCTURAL HARDWARECOMPOSITE PROPELLANTDOUBLE-BASE PROPELLANT

Six traps specific to motor analysis

Mesh quality — the numbers that decide whether a result is real

Every solver reports these. Most engineers never look at them, and a single bad element at a fillet can dominate the peak stress you report.

METRICIDEALGOODMARGINALREJECTWHY IT MATTERS

Element selection

ANALYSIS TASKUSEAVOIDREASON
THE FIRST-ORDER TETRAHEDRON PROBLEM 4-node tets are artificially stiff — they under-predict displacement and therefore under-predict stress, which is the dangerous direction. They are the default in most automatic meshers because they fill any geometry. If you must use tets, use second-order (10-node) ones. A first-order tet mesh that looks beautifully dense can still be wrong by 20–30% on a bending-dominated part.

Mesh convergence

Refine, plot, and report the convergence — not just the final number.

Physical test methods & FEA correlation

Model verification checklist

Run these before believing any result. Most bad FEA fails one of them, not the physics.

THE UNITS TRAP, SPECIFICALLY In the mm–N–tonne system almost every mm-based solver uses, density must be tonne/mm³: steel is 7.85e-9, not 7850 and not 7.85e-6. Get it wrong and modal frequencies and inertia loads are out by a factor of roughly 1000, while the static stress looks perfectly fine. The density register gives the correct figure in every unit.
SINGULARITIES ARE NOT STRESSES A sharp re-entrant corner, a point load or a fixed node produces a stress that rises without limit as you refine the mesh. It never converges because the true elastic solution is infinite there. Either model the real fillet radius, or assess the region by a method that does not depend on peak stress.
CORRELATE, THEN PREDICT An uncorrelated model is a hypothesis. Correlate against strain gauges or a modal survey first, understand any disagreement, and only then use it to predict conditions you have not tested.
MARGIN IS ONLY AS GOOD AS THE ALLOWABLE State which allowable you used and its statistical basis. A-basis, B-basis and typical values can differ by 20% or more, and a margin quoted against a typical value is not a margin at all.
DESIGN NOTES — DECISIONS, TRAPS AND CHECK SEQUENCES
FEA SETUP CHECKLIST — IN ONE LINE Check boundary conditions, reactions and convergence first — read stresses last.

Checklist, in order

  1. Units — consistent throughout. The most common silent error.
  2. Materials — correct properties at the right temperature; linear or nonlinear as appropriate.
  3. Elements — no linear tetrahedra in bending regions; use quadratic elements.
  4. Boundary conditions — model the real support. Fully fixed faces are stiffer than reality and create false stress peaks at the constraint.
  5. Contacts — bonded only where the parts really are bonded. Bolted joints usually need contact and preload.
  6. Reactions — sum the reaction forces; they must equal the applied loads.
  7. Deformed shape — exaggerate it and ask whether it looks physically right.
  8. Convergence — refine at the point of interest until the result changes by less than about 5%.
  9. Hand-calc comparison — see Hand calcs.
  10. Only now, read stresses.
TRAP Singularities. At sharp re-entrant corners, point loads and point constraints, stress rises without limit as the mesh refines. It isn't real and it doesn't converge. Model the real fillet, or assess with linearised stresses or a hot-spot method.

Pressure hardware

For pressure-retaining parts, linearise stresses through the thickness into membrane, membrane-plus-bending and peak, and assess each against its own limit — the approach used in pressure vessel codes such as ASME VIII Division 2.

Report must state

Software and version, units, element types and mesh size at critical areas, materials and their basis, loads and boundary conditions with justification, convergence evidence, and reaction balance.

⚠ Guidance for engineering judgement, not a substitute for a qualified stress analyst. Structural substantiation of flight or pressure hardware must be performed and signed off by the responsible stress authority under the governing programme requirements.

Tolerance stack-up

Build a dimension loop, get the worst-case and statistical result, and see which contributor is actually costing you the tolerance.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THE POINT IS NOT THE TOTAL — IT IS THE RANKING Any stack tells you whether the assembly closes. The useful output is which contributor dominates, because tightening anything else is wasted money. In an RSS stack, contribution scales with the square of the tolerance, so the largest contributor is disproportionately dominant — halving the biggest tolerance beats tightening three small ones.

Dimension loop

Result

—

Thermal expansion

Assign a material to any row and the stack is recomputed at temperature. CTE comes live from the material database.

GD&T in a linear stack

How each control converts to a ± contribution. Every conversion below is applied automatically when you pick a GD&T row.

THE FACTOR-OF-TWO ERROR A diametral zone is a circle, so only its radius acts along any one stack direction. Position Ø0.2 contributes ±0.1, not ±0.2. Using the full diameter doubles the apparent contribution and is the single most common GD&T mistake in stack-ups.
MMC BONUS BELONGS IN THE STACK When a position tolerance carries Ⓜ, the feature gains bonus tolerance as it departs from MMC — up to the full size tolerance band. Leaving it out makes the stack look tighter than it is and leads to tightening parts that never needed it. Only position controls accept a bonus; form and orientation controls cannot.

Monte Carlo & predicted defect rate

Worst case and RSS give you a band. Monte Carlo gives you a distribution and a number you can act on: how many assemblies actually fail.

Process capability reference

PROCESSTYPICAL ±NOTE

Contribution analysis

Where the variation actually comes from. Spend your tolerance budget at the top of this list.

CONTRIBUTORNOMINALTOLERANCEWORST-CASE SHARERSS SHARE
WHEN RSS IS NOT VALID RSS assumes contributors are independent and normally distributed. It is wrong for one-offs and small batches, for parts from the same mould cavity or bar, where a single setup drives several dimensions, or where a process is skewed or bimodal. If in doubt on a safety-critical fit, use worst case.
GD&T IN A LINEAR STACK A position tolerance of Ø0.2 contributes ±0.1 in any one direction, not ±0.2 — the diametral zone is a circle, and only its radius acts along your stack direction. Getting this wrong doubles the apparent contribution.
THE 50% RULE OF THUMB If one contributor exceeds roughly half the RSS variance, the stack is effectively controlled by that one dimension. Improve it before touching anything else — and consider whether a datum or design change removes it from the loop entirely.
THE FOUR MISTAKES THAT WRECK A STACK 1. A minus sign flips the nominal contribution, never the tolerance — tolerances always add. 2. Mixing equal-bilateral and limit dimensions without converting first; shift the nominal to an equal ± form before stacking. 3. Using RSS on a low-volume or uncentred process, where it over-promises badly. 4. Forgetting bonus tolerance at MMC — it belongs in the stack, and ignoring it makes you tighten parts that did not need it.
THE √n RULE RSS reduces the stack by roughly √n against worst case: 4 contributors gives about 50%, 16 gives about 75%. That is why splitting a tolerance across more features can help — and why a stack dominated by one large contributor never benefits from RSS.
CLOSE THE LOOP Every stack must form a closed chain from one face of the gap, through the parts, back to the other face. If the loop does not close, the answer is meaningless no matter how careful the arithmetic. Draw it before you calculate it.
ZONE 5

Metallurgy fundamentals

Why materials behave the way the selector says they do — crystal structure, strengthening mechanisms, and the transformation diagrams behind every temper and condition on the site.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THE THROUGH-LINE Every temper code, H-condition and heat treatment elsewhere on this site is a position on one of the diagrams below. T6 is the peak of the ageing curve; T73 is deliberately past it. A quench-and-temper condition is a path across the TTT curve. Once you can see that, the designation systems stop being arbitrary.

Crystal structure — and why it decides cryogenic behaviour

Drag any cell to rotate it. Atom positions are computed from fractional lattice coordinates, so the structures are correct by construction rather than drawn by hand.

THE MOST IMPORTANT CONSEQUENCE ON THIS WHOLE SITE BCC metals have a ductile-to-brittle transition; FCC metals do not. That single fact is why austenitic stainless, aluminium, copper and nickel are used at cryogenic temperature and ferritic steel is not — a carbon steel that is perfectly tough in the workshop can shatter like glass at −100 °C. It is also why the density register lists 9% Ni steel separately: the nickel suppresses the transition far enough to make a ferritic steel usable for LNG.

Iron–carbon phase diagram

The map underneath every steel on this site. Carbon content sets what phases can exist; temperature sets which of them actually do.

THE EUTECTOID POINT0.77% carbon at 727 °C is where austenite transforms directly to pearlite with no intermediate two-phase region. Steels below it are hypoeutectoid — ferrite plus pearlite — and that includes almost every structural and aerospace steel on this site.
WHY MOST STRUCTURAL STEEL SITS AT 0.3–0.5% CEnough carbon to form useful martensite on quenching, little enough to stay weldable and tough. Above roughly 0.5% the steel hardens more but cracks readily on welding and quenching — 4340 at 0.40% and 4130 at 0.30% are both deliberately in this window.

Time–temperature–transformation

What you actually get depends on how fast you cool through the nose of the curve. Same steel, three different materials.

HARDENABILITY IS NOT HARDNESSAlloying (Cr, Mo, Ni) pushes the curve right, giving more time to miss the nose. That is hardenability — the ability to harden deeper, not harder. Maximum hardness comes from carbon content alone. This is why 4340 through-hardens in thick section while plain carbon steel of the same carbon content does not.
THE THREE DESTINATIONSPearlite from slow cooling — soft, ductile, layered ferrite and cementite. Bainite from intermediate rates — a good strength/toughness balance, and the basis of austempering. Martensite from missing the nose entirely — a diffusionless shear to a body-centred tetragonal lattice, extremely hard and extremely brittle until tempered.

Precipitation hardening — the ageing curve

Where every T-temper and H-condition on this site actually sits.

WHY T73 EXISTS AND IS WEAKER ON PURPOSE7075-T6 sits at the peak. 7075-T73 is aged past it, giving up roughly 10–15% strength to buy a large gain in stress-corrosion resistance. The coarser, incoherent precipitates that cost you strength are also the ones that stop hydrogen and stress cracking the alloy. In the selector, T6 and T73 differ by exactly this trade.
OVER-AGEING IS ALSO WHAT HAPPENS IN SERVICEThe curve is a function of time and temperature. A peak-aged alloy held hot enough for long enough will walk down the right-hand side of this curve on its own. That is precisely what the temperature retention curves in the material selector are modelling.

Strengthening mechanisms

There are only six ways to make a metal stronger. Every alloy on this site uses one or more of them.

Heat treatments

TREATMENTWHAT HAPPENSWHY YOU WOULD SPECIFY IT

Surface finish & metrology

What each process can actually achieve, what finish each application needs, and why Ra on its own is not enough to specify a functional surface.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

EVERY STEP FINER COSTS REAL MONEY Going from Ra 3.2 to Ra 0.8 usually means adding a grinding operation. Going to Ra 0.1 means adding honing or lapping on top of that. Specify the roughest finish that works — over-specified surface finish is one of the most common and least noticed ways drawings become expensive, and it rarely gets questioned because it looks like diligence.

Process capability

Achievable Ra bands by process. Select a target and the chart shows which processes can reach it.

Target

Equivalents

—

Application guide

APPLICATIONTYPICAL RaWHY

Parameter relationships

Ra ALONE DOES NOT SPECIFY A FUNCTIONAL SURFACE Ra is an average. Two surfaces with identical Ra can have completely different peak structures — one a plateau with fine valleys, the other covered in sharp peaks. For seals, bearings and fatigue-critical faces, specify the parameter that matches the function: Rz or Rmr (bearing ratio), not just Ra.
DIRECTION MATTERS TOO Lay direction is part of the specification and is often the thing that actually fails. A dynamic seal running across a turned spiral will pump fluid along the groove and leak however good the Ra is. Specify the lay symbol, not just the number.
THE FATIGUE CONNECTION Surface finish is not cosmetic on a loaded part. It is the ka factor in the Marin fatigue correction in the GD&T zone — a ground surface at Ra 0.4 keeps roughly 90% of endurance strength, while an as-forged surface keeps about 35%. That is a 2.5× difference in fatigue life driver from finish alone.
MEASURE WHAT YOU SPECIFY Cut-off length and filter change the number. A roughness measurement without a stated cut-off is not comparable to anything. Also confirm the feature is accessible to a stylus — specifying Ra 0.4 inside a small blind bore may be unmeasurable in practice.
ZONE 55

Welding & joining

Process selection, the carbon-equivalent preheat decision, what actually goes wrong in a weld, and which materials fight back.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THE WELD IS NOT THE PARENT MATERIAL A fusion weld gives you three different materials in the same joint: weld metal, heat-affected zone, and unaffected parent. Design to the weakest of them. In 6082-T6 the HAZ drops to near-annealed strength — roughly half the parent yield — and it stays that way. Sizing a welded aluminium joint on parent properties is one of the most common and most expensive mistakes on this site's material list.

Carbon equivalent & preheat

Composition

Preheat assessment

—

Process selection

PROCESSTHICKNESSSPEEDQUALITYCOSTTYPICAL USE

Weldability by material

MATERIALWELDABILITYWHAT TO WATCH

Defects — cause and consequence

PLANAR DEFECTS ARE THE DANGEROUS ONES Lack of fusion and cracks are crack-like and behave as pre-existing flaws in a fracture assessment. Rounded porosity of the same volume is far less severe. This is why acceptance standards treat them completely differently — and why the critical flaw size in the case-sizing zone matters so much for a welded case.
RADIOGRAPHY CAN MISS THE WORST DEFECT A lack-of-fusion plane lying parallel to the X-ray beam may produce almost no image contrast. Ultrasonic inspection detects planar defects far more reliably. Choose the NDT method for the defect you fear, not for convenience.
DESIGN THE JOINT, NOT JUST THE WELD Move welds away from stress concentrations and fatigue-critical areas. The weld toe is a built-in notch — grinding it smooth or peening it can double fatigue life at almost no cost, and is usually cheaper than upsizing the section.
DISTORTION IS THE UNDER-ESTIMATED RISK It is not an NDT defect so it does not appear in acceptance criteria, yet it scraps more parts than porosity does. Balance the weld sequence, back-step, fixture properly, and leave machining stock on anything that must hold tolerance afterwards.
DESIGN NOTES — DECISIONS, TRAPS AND CHECK SEQUENCES
WELD & BRAZE DETAIL — IN ONE LINE Place welds where stress is low and inspection is easy — never in a fillet radius or at a stress peak.

Fusion welding

  • Strength — use the joint efficiency from the code and the qualified procedure. Parent-metal allowables don't apply to the weld or the heat-affected zone.
  • Heat-affected zone in aluminium — heat-treated 6xxx and 7xxx alloys lose temper next to the weld. HAZ yield can drop to around half the -T6 value or below.
  • Titanium — needs full inert shielding on both faces. Weld colour is an acceptance criterion: silver to light straw acceptable, blue and grey rejected under typical aerospace criteria.
  • Process — electron beam and laser give narrow welds and low distortion; TIG is flexible but puts in more heat.

Design rules

  1. Full-penetration welds in primary load paths; fillet welds are for secondary structure.
  2. Keep welds away from geometric stress raisers and from each other.
  3. Plan NDT access — radiography needs line of sight, ultrasonic needs a coupling surface.
  4. Machine critical features after welding; distortion is certain.
  5. Specify post-weld heat treatment where the alloy needs it.

Brazing

Capillary joints need controlled clearance, typically around 0.025–0.125 mm depending on filler — check the filler datasheet. Vacuum brazing avoids flux entrapment, which matters for anything that must be clean inside.

TRAP A weld symbol without a procedure, an acceptance standard and an inspection method is incomplete. The welder will use a house default.
⚠ Guidance for design decisions. Welding of pressure or flight hardware requires a qualified procedure (WPS/PQR to BS EN ISO 15614 or equivalent), qualified welders, and NDT to the governing acceptance standard such as BS EN ISO 5817.

NDT method selection & probability of detection

Choosing the inspection for the defect you actually fear, and checking that what you can detect is smaller than what will kill the part.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THE QUESTION THAT DECIDES EVERYTHING Not “what NDT shall we specify?” but “is my critical flaw size larger than what my inspection can reliably find?” If the critical flaw is smaller than the detectable flaw, you cannot inspect your way to safety — no amount of NDT makes that part safe, and the design must change. This is the single most important idea in fracture control and it is routinely missed.

Inspectability check

Your flaw

WHY A FACTORDamage-tolerance practice assumes the largest flaw that could be missed is present from day one. Requiring the critical size to exceed the detectable size by a margin is what makes the inspection meaningful rather than nominal.

Verdict

—

Detection capability

Indicative a90/95 — the flaw size found with 90% probability at 95% confidence. Your critical flaw size is marked.

Method comparison

METHODREACHa90/95MATERIALSSTANDARDFINDS / MISSES
POD IS A STATISTICAL STATEMENT, NOT A GUARANTEE a90/95 means 90% of flaws that size are found, with 95% confidence in that figure. It explicitly accepts that one in ten flaws at the detection limit is missed. That is why damage tolerance assumes a missed flaw is present rather than assuming inspection is perfect.
MATCH THE METHOD TO THE DEFECT ORIENTATION Radiography can miss a lack-of-fusion plane lying across the beam; magnetic particle misses cracks parallel to the field; ultrasonic misses flaws parallel to the beam. Every method has a blind orientation. Choose for the defect you expect from the process, which is what the welding zone tells you.
SURFACE CONDITION CHANGES EVERYTHING Penetrant needs a genuinely clean, open surface — machining or shot peening can smear metal across a crack and hide it entirely. Etching before penetrant is standard practice on machined fracture-critical parts for exactly this reason.
PERSONNEL QUALIFICATION IS PART OF THE SPECIFICATION NDT results depend on the operator as much as the equipment. Aerospace work requires certification to NAS 410 or EN 4179 at the appropriate level. An uncertified inspection is not evidence.
DESIGN NOTES — DECISIONS, TRAPS AND CHECK SEQUENCES
INSPECTION & NDT — IN ONE LINE Choose the NDT method by the smallest flaw that must be found — which comes from fracture analysis, not habit.

Methods

MethodFindsBlind to
PenetrantSurface-breaking cracks, porositySubsurface; cracks smeared shut
Magnetic particleSurface and near-surface, ferrous onlyAustenitic stainless, Al, Ti
Eddy currentSurface and near-surface cracks, conductive metals; good in bolt holesDeep defects; needs calibration standards
UltrasonicPlanar subsurface defects, thicknessDefects parallel to the beam
RadiographyVolumetric — porosity, inclusionsTight cracks normal to the beam
CTInternal geometry, additive porositySize, density, cost

Link to fracture control

For fracture-critical parts, fracture analysis gives the largest flaw that can survive the service life. The NDT method must reliably detect flaws smaller than that — with demonstrated probability of detection. If no practical method can, the options are a proof test that screens out the critical flaw size, a redesign, or a lower stress.

Leak testing

MethodApproximate sensitivity
Bubble test≈10⁻³–10⁻⁴ mbar·L/s
Pressure decay≈10⁻³–10⁻⁴ mbar·L/s, volume-dependent
Helium mass spectrometerdown to ≈10⁻⁹ mbar·L/s and below

State the allowable leak rate, test gas, pressure and method. “No leaks” is not a requirement — every seal leaks at some rate.

TRAP Penetrant after machining or shot peening can miss real cracks because the metal is smeared over them. Etch first, or inspect before the smearing operation.

What a callout must carry

  • Method and sensitivity level
  • Acceptance standard and class
  • Coverage — surfaces and depth
  • Process stage — before or after machining and surface treatment
