ZONE 15

Cryogenic design

Material suitability, contraction and the two things that will actually bite you: the ductile-to-brittle transition, and titanium in oxygen.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

CRYSTAL STRUCTURE DECIDES THIS, NOT STRENGTH FCC metals have no ductile-to-brittle transition; BCC metals do. That single fact from the metallurgy zone governs almost every cryogenic material decision. Austenitic stainless, aluminium, copper and nickel stay tough to liquid helium temperature and get stronger as they cool. A carbon steel that is perfectly tough in the workshop can fracture like glass at −100 °C. Choose on structure first, strength second.

Contraction calculator

Component

Contraction

—

Material suitability by crystal structure

Liquid oxygen compatibility

In LOX the question is ignition, not strength.

MATERIALLOX SERVICENOTE
THE TITANIUM TRAP Titanium has the best specific strength in the database and is prohibited in liquid oxygen. It reacts violently with LOX and can ignite from impact or from a fresh scratch exposing bare metal. The material selector will happily rank Ti-6Al-4V first for a pressure vessel — if that vessel holds LOX, the answer is wrong. No performance index catches this.
FITS CHANGE ON COOLDOWN A clearance fit at room temperature is not a clearance fit at 20 K if the two parts are different materials. An aluminium housing on a steel shaft tightens by roughly 0.2% of diameter over that range. Size the fit at temperature, not on the bench — The fits and limits zone gives the room-temperature limits; this zone gives the movement.
HYDROGEN IS TWO PROBLEMS AT ONCE Liquid hydrogen brings cryogenic temperature and hydrogen embrittlement. Embrittlement of austenitic stainless is worst around 200 K rather than at the coldest point, so a system that is fine at 20 K can be damaged during chilldown and warm-up. Metastable grades like 304L are the most affected because strain-induced martensite forms on deformation.
COMPOSITES MICROCRACK BEFORE THEY BREAK Carbon/epoxy gains strength and stiffness cold, but the resin contracts far more than the fibre and the mismatch drives transverse microcracking. The cracks open permeation paths long before any structural failure — this is what ended the X-33 composite LH2 tank programme, and why liners and toughened resins exist.
CLEANLINESS IS A STRUCTURAL REQUIREMENT IN LOX Hydrocarbons in liquid oxygen are an explosion hazard. LOX hardware is cleaned to a specified particulate and non-volatile-residue level, assembled with oxygen-compatible lubricants only, and kept sealed. A perfectly designed part contaminated with cutting fluid is a hazard.
⚠ Contraction values are integrated figures for material classes, adequate for sizing and screening. Take alloy-specific data from NIST cryogenic property databases or the material specification for final design, and confirm LOX compatibility by the governing standard such as ASTM G93 and G72.
ZONE 36

FEA material cards

Elastic constants, a Ramberg-Osgood plasticity table in Abaqus format, and an estimated S-N curve — at your design temperature.

READ THIS BEFORE YOU PASTE ANYTHING INTO A SOLVER None of the curves below are test data. They are generated from the published monotonic properties this site holds — E, Rp0.2 and Rm — using standard models. Three tiers, marked on every value:
  • EXACT — the engineering-to-true conversion. Pure mathematics, no assumption.
  • DERIVED — the Ramberg-Osgood curve, computed from properties held in the database.
  • ESTIMATED — the hardening exponent n and the S-N curve. Class-typical values, not measurements.
Use these to get a model running and to explore sensitivity. Replace n and the curve with MMPDS, CMH-17 or your own coupon data before any analysis anyone relies on. Where a material cannot be honestly represented by these models, this page says so and gives you nothing rather than guessing.

Material & condition

Elastic constants

—

Stress–strain curve

Abaqus material card

Copy straight into an input deck. Units are N, mm, MPa, tonne — density is in tonne/mm³, the trap the FEA zone warns about.

—

Estimated S-N curve

Basquin fit between a 0.9×Rm anchor at 10³ cycles and the Marin-corrected endurance limit. An estimate, not test data.

WHERE RAMBERG-OSGOOD IS A POOR MODEL Mild steel with a Lüders plateau yields at constant stress — RO cannot represent that at all. Annealed austenitic stainless hardens so heavily that a single exponent fits badly across the whole range. Magnesium has strong tension-compression asymmetry that no isotropic model captures. In all three cases use a measured curve.
THE CURVE STOPS AT ULTIMATE FOR A REASON Beyond the ultimate point the specimen necks and the engineering stress-strain relationship stops being a material property — it becomes a structural response of that specimen. Abaqus needs true stress against true plastic strain up to necking; past that you need a corrected curve from a Bridgman analysis or inverse FE fitting.
TEMPERATURE SCALING Strength is scaled by the retention curves from the material selector — the same validated model the selector and case sizing use. Modulus is scaled by a smaller factor, since E falls more slowly than yield for most metals. Both are estimates: at temperature, get real data.
FOR A TIME-DEPENDENT MATERIAL, THIS IS THE WRONG CARD Everything on this page is rate-independent plasticity. Polymers, elastomers, propellant grains and bondlines are viscoelastic — their stiffness depends on how fast you load them and how long you wait. A plasticity table cannot express that at any number of points. The viscoelasticity zone generates the *VISCOELASTIC, TIME=PRONY card you need instead, with the WLF shift for temperature.
WHAT IS GENUINELY EXACT HERE The engineering→true conversion is σtrue = σ(1+ε) and εtrue = ln(1+ε), with plastic strain εpl = εtrue − σtrue/E. No assumptions, and it is the step most often got wrong when hand-building a card.
⚠ Screening and model-setup aid only. Design allowables and material cards for released analysis must come from MMPDS, CMH-17, the governing specification, or your own qualified test programme.

Viscoelasticity

Why some materials answer “solid or liquid?” with “how long are you watching?” — the models, the experiments, and the card that goes into a solver.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THE ONE SENTENCE VERSION In an elastic material stress depends on strain. In a viscoelastic material stress depends on the whole history of strain — on how fast you got there and how long you have been waiting. Every complication in this zone follows from that one change.
WHERE THIS LEADS The molecular sandbox shows the mechanism behind these curves, and the propellant grain zone applies all of it to real hardware — grain margin, bondlines and storage life.

Ten ways of seeing it

MODELRELAXATIONCREEPGOOD FOR / FAILS AT

The two experiments

Everything is measured one of two ways, and they are mirror images of each other.

Controls

—

Watch it happen — creep and relaxation

The two experiments, run on the same material. Pick a model and see why the classical ones are not enough.

Experiment

What the model says

—

The master curve — heat as a time machine

Short tests at several temperatures, slid along the time axis until they overlap into one curve spanning far longer than any test.

Prony series — straight into a solver

The generalised Maxwell coefficients in Abaqus form, with the WLF constants supplied as a thermorheologically simple shift.

—
gᵢ ARE NORMALISED, AND MUST SUM TO LESS THAN 1 Abaqus wants dimensionless relaxation moduli: gᵢ = Eᵢ / E₀, where E₀ is the instantaneous modulus. The remainder 1 − Σgᵢ is the long-term fraction. If Σgᵢ reaches 1 the material relaxes completely and the solver will reject it — a common error when a fit is scaled wrongly.
THE ELASTIC CARD MUST MATCH Give *ELASTIC the instantaneous modulus, not the room-temperature datasheet value, or state MODULI=LONG TERM and give the relaxed one. Mixing the two is the other common error, and it silently scales every stress in the model.

Dynamic mechanical analysis

Push it sinusoidally. What comes back is E′, what turns to heat is E″, and the ratio finds the transitions.

Molecular sandbox — a live simulation

Real Langevin dynamics: beads joined by springs, with excluded volume so chains genuinely cannot pass through one another. Move the cursor over the box to push the molecules around. Drag to rotate the view.

WHAT THIS IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT This is a qualitative sandbox, not a quantitative model. It honestly shows thermal motion scaling with temperature, plasticiser moving faster than the chains it lubricates, a star polymer diffusing slower than a linear one, chains blocking one another, and binder dewetting from filler particles. It does not reproduce elastic recovery: the bonds here are enthalpic springs, while real rubber elasticity is entropic — chains recoil because a coiled state has more entropy, and nothing in this model represents that. I tested for recovery across damping and crosslink density and it does not appear, so the page does not claim it.

Propellant grain

Viscoelasticity applied to hardware: what a double-base grain is structurally, whether it survives cold soak, whether the bondline holds, and what twenty years of storage does to both.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

SCOPE This zone covers the mechanical and structural behaviour of the grain — the same discipline as NASA SP-8073, and the reason a grain does or does not survive storage. Formulation, energetics, burn rate and internal ballistics are outside the scope of this site.

Double-base propellant

SCOPE This section covers the mechanical and structural behaviour of the material — the same discipline as NASA SP-8073, and the reason a grain does or does not survive storage. Formulation, energetics, burn rate and internal ballistics are outside the scope of this site.

A double-base propellant is, structurally, a plasticised polymer: a nitrocellulose backbone with nitroglycerine acting as plasticiser. The NC is the structural material; everything above applies to it directly, and rather strongly — heavily plasticised cellulosics are among the most temperature-sensitive engineering polymers there are.

Three relaxations, not one

DMA on double-base propellant finds three distinct transitions. Which one you call Tg changes every shift factor you compute.

Three states

Bondline stress

Interfacial shear from thermal mismatch. It is not uniform — it concentrates at free edges, which is why debonds start at terminations.

Stack

Bond margin

—

Ageing & storage life

Arrhenius kinetics on a single dominant mechanism — what an accelerated test actually proves, and how the properties drift meanwhile.

Programme

What the test proves

—

Grain structural margin

Bore strain from cure cool-down and from pressurisation, against capability at temperature.

Motor

Margin

—

Grain structural load cases

LOAD CASEWHAT IT ISWHY IT MATTERS
WHY CRACKING IS A SAFETY PROBLEM, NOT A PERFORMANCE ONE A crack in a grain is new burning surface. More surface means more gas generated per second, which means higher chamber pressure, which can mean the case fails. That is why grain structural integrity is treated as a safety discipline and why cold-soak cracking is taken so seriously — the structural failure and the pressure excursion are the same event.
AN ELASTIC ANALYSIS GIVES THE WRONG ANSWER TWICE Use slow-test data on a fast event like ignition and you under-predict stiffness and stress. Use fast data on a slow event like cure cool-down and you over-predict stress, because months of relaxation genuinely bleed it away. Viscoelastic analysis is not a refinement here — the elastic answer is wrong in a different direction for each load case.
AGEING MOVES THE CURVES Over decades of storage, plasticiser migrates and evaporates and stabiliser is consumed. The material stiffens, tan δ falls and the transitions shift. A propellant characterised when new is not the material you have at twenty years, which is why storage-life prediction is done by tracking modulus and transition temperature rather than by chemistry alone.
PRONY SERIES GO STRAIGHT INTO A SOLVER The generalised Maxwell coefficients are what Abaqus wants for *VISCOELASTIC, TIME=PRONY, with the WLF constants supplied separately for temperature dependence. A fit is only valid over the time and temperature range it was fitted to — extrapolate it and you are inventing data.
⚠ Screening only. The Prony spectrum, WLF constants and propellant properties used here are illustrative of the behaviour, not measurements of any real material. Grain structural analysis requires characterisation of the actual material to the governing programme requirements.

ZONE 27

Ablative liners

How thick a nozzle liner or case insulator has to be: what erodes away, and what has to stay cool behind it.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

AN ABLATIVE DOES TWO JOBS AT ONCE It sacrifices its surface — pyrolysing, charring and receding, carrying heat away with the mass it loses — and it insulates what is behind it. Size for only the first and the structure cooks; size for only the second and the liner burns through. The thickness you need is both, plus margin.
HEAT FLUX IS AN INPUT, NOT AN OUTPUT This site does not compute heat flux — that comes from your own ballistic and gas-dynamic analysis. Enter what your analysis gives you. Everything below is the thermal and materials consequence of that number.

Duty

Required thickness

—

Why the two jobs pull in opposite directions

LOW RECESSION DOES NOT MEAN GOOD INSULATION Carbon-carbon and graphite barely erode, and conduct heat a hundred times better than carbon phenolic. They protect the surface superbly and the structure hardly at all. A graphite throat insert almost always needs a separate insulator behind it.
PENETRATION GROWS AS √t Doubling the burn time increases thermal penetration by √2, not 2. A long-burn motor is less punishing per second than the arithmetic suggests — but recession is linear in time, so the balance between the two shifts as duration grows.
WHAT IS EXACT HERE Thermal penetration is x = 3.64√(αt), the depth at which the temperature rise falls to 1% of the surface step in a semi-infinite solid, with α = k/ρcp. No fitting, no assumption beyond the idealisation.
WHAT IS NOT Recession rate is an estimate. It depends on flux, gas composition, particle loading, shear and the specific material lay-up — none of which this site knows. The default scales with flux from a class-typical datum. Replace it with a measured rate from your own firings or supplier data before sizing anything real.
⚠ Preliminary sizing aid. A real nozzle liner is sized with a transient thermal model using measured material response, and confirmed by test. Char, pyrolysis-gas blowing and in-depth reactions are not modelled here.
ZONE 32

Shell buckling

Thin shells fail far below their theoretical strength. How far below, and when it governs at all.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THIS IS WHY EIGENVALUE BUCKLING IS ALWAYS UNCONSERVATIVE A linear eigenvalue analysis solves the perfect shell. Real shells have out-of-roundness, weld shrinkage, thickness variation and handling dents, and a cylinder in axial compression is extraordinarily sensitive to them. A slender case skirt can carry less than a quarter of the classical value. The knockdown below is the industry's answer, and it is empirical: a lower bound fitted to test data, not a physical law.

Shell

Allowable

—
THE KNOCKDOWN IS A LOWER BOUND, NOT A PREDICTION SP-8007's curve was drawn beneath a scatter of test results from the 1960s, much of it on shells built to standards a modern filament-wound or friction-stir case would beat comfortably. It is safe and often very conservative. Programmes that can afford the testing measure their own imperfection sensitivity instead.
AXIAL AND EXTERNAL PRESSURE ARE DIFFERENT PROBLEMS Axial compression scales with t/r and is imperfection-dominated. External pressure scales with (t/r)³ — far more sensitive to wall thickness, and much less sensitive to imperfections. A shell comfortable in one can be marginal in the other.
CHECK WHETHER IT GOVERNS AT ALL For a thick enough wall the buckling allowable exceeds yield, and the shell simply yields first. The tool says which mode governs — running a buckling analysis on a part that yields first is effort spent on the wrong failure.
WHAT TO DO WHEN IT GOVERNS Thicken the wall, shorten the unsupported length, or add rings or stringers. Stiffening is usually far lighter than thickening, because the classical stress rises only linearly with t while mass rises linearly too — a ring buys stability for very little mass.
⚠ Preliminary sizing. Real buckling assessment uses measured imperfection data, non-linear analysis with realistic geometry, and test. Boundary conditions, unsupported length and combined loading all matter and are not modelled here.
ZONE 33

Leak before break

When a crack finally goes through the wall, does the vessel hiss — or does it come apart?

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THE SAFEST FAILURE IS ONE YOU CAN HEAR A crack growing in service eventually reaches the back face. If it penetrates before it goes critical, the vessel leaks: pressure drops, the leak is detectable, and the failure is benign. If it goes critical while still buried, the crack runs and the vessel bursts with no warning at all. Which of the two you get is a design decision, whether or not anyone made it deliberately.

Vessel

Verdict

—

Every material at this duty

A THICKER WALL CAN MAKE THINGS WORSE Thickening a wall lowers stress, which helps — but it also means a crack must grow further before it breaks through. Past a certain thickness the flaw reaches critical size while still buried, and a vessel that would have leaked now bursts instead. Leak-before-break is a property of the wall relative to the toughness, not of the material alone.
IT IS AN ARGUMENT, NOT A CALCULATION A real leak-before-break case has to show that the leak is detectable in time to act — leak rate, detection method, crew or system response. A vessel that leaks into a sealed compartment nobody monitors has gained very little. This tool answers only the fracture-mechanics half.
IT PAIRS WITH INSPECTION, NOT INSTEAD OF IT If leak-before-break holds, a missed flaw leaks rather than bursts — which is exactly the defence you want when NDT cannot reliably find the critical size. Check both together: the case sizing zone gives the critical flaw, the NDT zone gives what you can find, and this zone gives what happens if you miss it.
HIGH-STRENGTH ALLOYS FAIL THIS TEST Toughness generally falls as strength rises. A maraging or 7075 case sized to a high working stress can have a critical flaw smaller than its own wall — there is no leak path, only a burst. That is the real cost of chasing strength, and it does not appear anywhere in a static stress margin.
⚠ Linear-elastic screening only. A released leak-before-break argument uses J-integral or R-curve analysis, measured toughness at temperature and orientation, realistic flaw shapes, and a demonstrated leak-detection route. ASME and NASA-STD-5019 set the real requirements.
ZONE 35

Proof testing

A proof test does not demonstrate that a vessel is sound. It sorts the ones that are from the ones that are not — and tells you how long the survivors have.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

PROOF IS A SORTING OPERATION Any vessel carrying a flaw large enough to fail at proof pressure fails during the test — safely, on the ground, with nobody near it. Every survivor therefore carries a flaw smaller than the critical size at proof pressure. That is not a statement about workmanship; it is a guarantee produced by the test itself, and it holds even for flaws no inspection could find.

Test & duty

What the test buys

—
THE PROOF TEST ITSELF GROWS CRACKS Pressurising to proof applies the single largest stress the vessel will ever see. It can extend a sub-critical flaw, and in a susceptible material it can leave the vessel worse than it found it. This is why proof pressures are kept as low as the argument allows, and why repeated proofing is not a substitute for inspection.
A HIGHER PROOF RATIO BUYS LIFE AS R² Because critical flaw size goes as 1/σ², raising the proof ratio shrinks the guaranteed flaw as 1/R² — and the smaller starting flaw then takes longer to grow. The gain is real but it is bought against the risk above, and against losing good hardware in the test.
IT COVERS WHAT INSPECTION CANNOT NDT finds flaws down to its detection limit and no further. A proof test screens by consequence rather than by detection — it does not care whether the flaw was findable. Where the critical size sits below what NDT can reliably see, proof is the argument that remains.
THE GROWTH LAW IS THE WEAK LINK Everything after the screened flaw size rests on Paris constants that vary with environment, frequency, temperature, R-ratio and orientation. They are class-typical estimates here. Hydrogen, salt water or elevated temperature can move the life by an order of magnitude.
⚠ Screening only. A released proof-test argument uses measured toughness and growth data at the service condition, realistic flaw shapes, and the governing standard's factors — NASA-STD-5019 and the AIAA S-080/S-081 series set the requirements for flight pressure vessels.
ZONE 46

Residual stress

Stress the part carries with no load applied at all — and which decides how long it lasts.

IT IS NOT A LOAD, SO IT NEVER APPEARS IN A LOAD CASE Residual stress is locked in by manufacturing: machining, grinding, welding, forming, heat treatment. It does not show up in a static margin, it is rarely measured, and it routinely decides whether a part reaches its design life. Compressive residual buys fatigue life; tensile residual spends it — and welding leaves tensile residual approaching yield.

Surface condition

What it costs or buys

—

Where it comes from

A COMPRESSIVE LAYER IS ONLY AS DEEP AS IT IS Peening protects the first few tenths of a millimetre. A crack that grows past the layer sees the full applied stress again, and the benefit ends abruptly. Peening a component whose critical flaw is deeper than the layer buys initiation life and nothing else.
IT RELAXES Residual stress is not permanent. Thermal exposure, overload and cyclic plasticity all shed it — peening benefit measured on a new coupon may not survive service. Anything relying on residual stress needs to show it is still there at end of life.
MACHINING IT AWAY REMOVES THE BALANCE, NOT JUST THE STRESS A residual field is self-equilibrating. Remove material and the remainder re-equilibrates — which is why thin machined parts distort after the last cut, and why rough-machine, stress-relieve, finish-machine exists as a sequence.
THE NUMBERS HERE ARE RANGES, NOT VALUES Residual stress depends on the specific process parameters, geometry and material condition. The ranges below are indicative. If a design depends on residual stress, it must be measured — X-ray diffraction, hole drilling or neutron diffraction — not assumed.
⚠ Screening only. Residual stress fields are three-dimensional, vary through thickness, and redistribute under load. This page treats a single surface value against a mean-stress criterion, which is a first approximation and no more.
ZONE 6

Fatigue

Why parts fail at loads they survived the first thousand times — and how the pieces scattered across this site fit together.

A STATIC MARGIN CANNOT SEE THIS COMING A part can pass every static check with room to spare and still fail in service, because fatigue is damage from repetition, not from magnitude. The load that breaks it is often a fraction of the one it survived on day one. Everything below exists because that first sentence is true and deeply unintuitive.

Eight ways of seeing it

In order — each one sets up the next.

From a laboratory number to your part

Published endurance data comes from a polished coupon. Your part is none of those things. Drag the sliders to see what survives the journey.

Knockdowns

Roughness is a stress raiser and a crack starter. Ground is kind, as-forged is brutal.
A bigger section holds more surface, more inclusions and more chances to start.
Axial loading has no stress gradient to arrest an early crack, so it is worse than bending.
Above roughly a third of the melting point, creep and oxidation join in.
Moving from a 50% mean life to a 99.9% survival allowable.

What reaches the part

—

The S-N curve, and why aluminium is different

Mean stress — the same amplitude, very different life

Scatter — a life is a distribution, not a number

WHERE THE REST OF THIS LIVES The material selector applies the Marin factors and shows the corrected endurance for every alloy. FEA cards generate an S-N curve for a solver. Residual stress shows the mean-stress shift peening buys. Surface finish gives the roughness that sets ka. This zone is what connects them.
INITIATION AND PROPAGATION ARE DIFFERENT PROBLEMS Everything on this page is initiation — stress-life, for a part with no known flaw. Once a crack exists, stress-life stops applying and you switch to fracture mechanics: the proof testing zone integrates Paris growth from a known flaw. Using the wrong one is a common and expensive mistake.
THE CHEAPEST FATIGUE FIX IS USUALLY THE SURFACE Because cracks start at the surface, improving it is disproportionately effective. Polishing, peening or rolling a fatigue-critical feature often buys more life than a material change, at a fraction of the cost and with no requalification of the alloy.
THESE ARE ESTIMATES, AND FATIGUE PUNISHES OPTIMISM The Marin factors are correlations, the criteria are curve fits, and scatter is a factor of ten. A fatigue-critical part is qualified by test, not by calculation. Use this to size and to understand; use coupons and full-scale testing to substantiate.
⚠ Teaching and screening. Real fatigue substantiation uses material-specific S-N or ε-N data at the correct R-ratio, environment and temperature, a validated damage model, and test evidence at component level.
ZONE 34

Random vibration

A motor is carried long before it fires. What the ride does to it, and whether it survives qualification.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

THE RIDE IS OFTEN WORSE THAN THE FIRING A motor spends minutes firing and possibly hours strapped to a vehicle. Random vibration is broadband and statistical — there is no single load to check, only a spectrum and a duration. It routinely sizes brackets, attachments and internal hardware that the pressure case never troubles.

Environment & item

Response

—

Three-sigma damage — where the life actually goes

MILES ASSUMES ONE MODE AND A FLAT SPECTRUM It is a single-degree-of-freedom answer. Real hardware has many modes, spectra have breakpoints and notches, and the PSD at your resonance may be nothing like the plateau value. Use Miles to size and to sanity-check; use a modal or random-response FEA, and then a shaker, to substantiate.
STIFFER IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY BETTER Response goes as √fn, so raising the natural frequency increases g-response even as it reduces deflection. The reason to push fn up is to clear the input spectrum or to avoid coupling with the vehicle — not to reduce the number of g.
DAMPING IS THE STRONGEST LEVER YOU HAVE Response goes as √Q, and Q is the one term you can change by an order of magnitude. A bolted joint with some friction may reach ζ = 5%; a machined monolithic bracket might be 1%, which is 2.2× the response for the same input.
RANDOM IS NOT SINUSOIDAL There is no single peak. The response is Gaussian, so the item spends 4.3% of its time above 2σ and briefly exceeds 3σ. Designing to the RMS value alone understates the peaks by a factor of three, which is why qualification is written around 3σ and why the damage sum below is banded rather than single-valued.
⚠ Screening. Real qualification follows the governing standard — MIL-STD-810, NASA-STD-7001 or the programme's own tailored spectrum — with measured modal data and a shaker test. Miles' equation is a first estimate, not a substantiation.
ZONE 28

Transient thermal

How fast something heats or cools — and when treating it as one temperature stops being honest.

THE STRUCTURE IS OFTEN HOTTEST AFTER THE MOTOR STOPS During firing the liner takes the heat. When firing ends, the gas stops moving but the insulation keeps releasing what it stored — inward, because that is the only direction left. Soak-back regularly peaks minutes after burnout, and it is what cooks bond lines, seals and electronics that survived the burn itself.

Mental models

The parts of this that are most often got wrong, pictured before they are calculated.

Part & environment

Response

—
ONE NUMBER: THE BIOT NUMBER Bi = hLc/k compares how fast heat arrives at the surface with how fast it spreads inside. Below 0.1 the interior keeps up and a single temperature is a fair description. Above it the part has a real gradient, and every figure on this page becomes a fiction — which is exactly when a quench cracks things.
τ IS A PROPERTY OF THE PART AND ITS SURROUNDINGS τ = ρcpLc/h. Thicker, denser or higher-capacity means slower; a more aggressive environment means faster. Conductivity does not appear — in the lumped regime the inside is already keeping up, so the bottleneck is entirely at the surface.
THREE TIME CONSTANTS IS 95% The approach is exponential, so it never quite arrives: 63% of the gap closes in one τ, 95% in three, 99.3% in five. Quoting a “time to reach” the environment temperature is meaningless — only time to reach a stated limit has an answer.
Lc IS THE WEAKEST INPUT Characteristic length is volume over surface area, which is unambiguous for a slab and a judgement call for anything real. A fin, a boss or a joint changes it locally. Get Lc wrong by two and you get τ wrong by two.
⚠ Screening. Real transient analysis uses a finite-element or finite-difference model with temperature-dependent properties, radiation where it matters, contact resistance at joints, and measured film coefficients. Lumped capacitance is a first estimate that tells you whether a detailed model is even needed.
ZONE 19

Silicone & polyurethane

Two elastomers with opposite chemistry, both everywhere in a motor — and a mutual incompatibility that ruins hardware quietly.

THEY POISON EACH OTHER, AND IT LOOKS LIKE BAD MATERIAL Polyurethane cures with amine and tin catalysts. Addition-cure silicone cures on platinum, which those catalysts poison at parts-per-million. The silicone simply never cures where they meet — and the usual conclusion is a bad batch of silicone rather than contamination. Meanwhile silicone's very low surface energy means it migrates everywhere and stops anything else bonding at all.

The two backbones, in 3D

Drag either model to rotate. Every property below follows from the shape of the chain.

Platinum poisoning, simulated

Drag the contamination level. Every green dot is a platinum site that can still catalyse the silicone cure; every amber dot is an amine or tin molecule migrating out of the urethane.

Contamination

WHY PARTS PER MILLION IS ENOUGH The platinum catalyst is itself present at parts per million. A poison only has to match the catalyst concentration, not the bulk — which is why a trace of urethane residue on a glove or a mould kills a whole batch.

Where they fight

Each with the actual mechanism, not just the warning.

ONE BOND EXPLAINS MOST OF SILICONE Si–O is 452 kJ/mol against carbon–carbon's 348, and the Si–O–Si angle opens to 143° rather than 109°. Stronger bond, floppier chain: high temperature capability and flexibility to −100 °C. The same open coiling is why gases walk straight through it.
ONE BOND EXPLAINS MOST OF POLYURETHANE The urethane linkage carries an N–H that hydrogen-bonds to its neighbour's carbonyl, pulling hard segments into stiff domains inside a soft matrix. That two-phase structure gives the abrasion and tear resistance — and the same bond is hydrolysable, which is the material's main weakness.
HOW TO KEEP THEM APART Separate storage and separate tooling. Cure polyurethane fully before silicone goes anywhere near it. Use a neutral-cure silicone, never acetoxy, next to metal or urethane. Where a joint between them is unavoidable, use a dedicated primer and expect mechanical interlock to do the work.
TEST THE COMBINATION, NOT THE MATERIALS Both may be perfectly qualified alone and still fail together. A small cure-compatibility coupon — silicone cast against the actual cured urethane, from the actual batch — costs an afternoon and catches platinum poisoning before it reaches hardware.
⚠ General elastomer chemistry for design awareness. Specific grades vary enormously — addition-cure and condensation-cure silicones behave differently, as do polyester and polyether urethanes. Confirm compatibility with the actual products and their datasheets, and by test.

ZONE 2

Requirements & interface control

Turn every “shall” into a numbered requirement with a verification method before any geometry exists.

A requirement you can't verify is an opinion. The first job on any new part is to convert the spec into a compliance matrix: one row per requirement, each with how it will be proven.

Verification methods

MethodUse forEvidence
TestAnything with a pass/fail measurable under loadTest report against a released procedure
AnalysisStrength, stiffness, thermal, where test is impracticalStress report with margins
InspectionDimensions, markings, finish, materialInspection record, certificate
DemonstrationAssembly, access, operabilityWitnessed record

Words that make a requirement unverifiable

WordingProblemRewrite as
“suitable”, “adequate”No thresholdThe number it must meet
“minimise”, “maximise”No end pointA limit, plus a goal if wanted
“as required”, “where necessary”Delegates the decisionThe specific condition
“and/or”Two requirements in oneSplit into two rows
“should”Non-binding in most specs“shall”, or move to guidance
DESIGN RULE Track TBD and TBC items in the same matrix with an owner and a date. A TBD that reaches drawing release becomes whatever the designer assumed on the day.

Derived requirements

Most of what governs a detail part is derived, not stated: a seal requirement becomes a surface finish, a flatness and a squeeze range. Write the derived ones down and trace them to their parent. When the parent changes, you can then find every feature it drives.

Interface control

IN ONE LINE Both sides design to the interface control document — never to the other team's current CAD.

Interfaces fail at the boundary between teams, not at the boundary between parts. The ICD is the only thing both teams can be held to.

What an ICD has to define

FieldContent
GeometryMating features, datum reference frame shared by both sides
Tolerance splitHow the allowable mismatch is divided between the two parts
LoadsForces and moments across the interface, both directions, all cases
ThermalTemperature each side, heat flow, allowable differential growth
SealingWhich side carries the groove, which the face, finish and flatness
FastenersWho supplies them, size, grade, torque and lubricant
Bonding / earthingElectrical continuity requirement and surface prep
Freeze dateWhen it stops moving, and the change route after that
TRAP Designing to the other team's live model. It feels efficient until they move a hole for their own reasons and nobody tells you. If it isn't in the ICD, it isn't agreed.
DESIGN RULE The mating datum schemes on both drawings must be the same features in the same order. If one side datums on the spigot and the other on the bolt circle, the tolerance stack across the interface is undefined.
⚠ Screening guidance from general practice. Ranges are typical, not allowables — confirm against the governing standard, your programme specification and company procedures before anything reaches a released drawing.
CHECK ALONGSIDE
ZONE 3

Duty cycle & environment

Count the real pressure and thermal cycles — single-use hardware still sees proof, leak and acceptance tests before it ever flies.

Most structural failures traced back in review started here, with a load case nobody wrote down. This zone exists to stop detail design opening before the environment is agreed.

What must be on the sheet before detail design opens

InputWhy it governsCommon miss
MEOP (max expected operating pressure)Sets wall and joint sizingQuoted nominal, not worst-case hot
Pressure rise rateDynamic load factor on joints and sealsTreated as static
Temperature: soak and transientKnockdowns, seal state, differential growthOnly steady-state given
Duration at temperatureShort- vs long-time allowables, creepNever asked for
Vibration and shock spectraPreload retention, fatigue, frettingDeferred to qualification
Handling and transportFrequently exceeds operating loadsIgnored
Assembly cyclesThread wear, inserts, seal reuseAssumed one
Storage life and conditionsElastomer ageing, corrosion, compression setTreated as packaging

Count the cycles honestly

“Single use” describes the mission, not the hardware's life. A pressure part typically sees development pressure checks, a proof test, one or more leak checks, acceptance testing, and sometimes rework and re-proof — before its one operational cycle. Each is a full stress cycle on every joint and seal.

EventTypical countNote
Proof test1–2Highest stress the part will ever see
Leak checks2–5Each disassembly adds one
Acceptance / functional1–3Programme-dependent
Thermal cycles in storagemanyDiurnal swings on seals and preload
DESIGN RULE If an input is unknown, write the assumption on the sheet with a name against it. An assumption with an owner gets challenged; a blank gets filled in silently by whoever is drawing at the time.

Limit, ultimate, proof

  • Limit — highest load expected in service. No factor applied.
  • Ultimate — limit × the factor from your programme spec. Must not rupture.
  • Proof — acceptance test level on delivered hardware, from the contract or code.

Factors come from the customer specification or governing code — never from a handbook default.

⚠ Screening guidance from general practice. Ranges are typical, not allowables — confirm against the governing standard, your programme specification and company procedures before anything reaches a released drawing.

ZONE 4

Criticality & DFMEA

Classify criticality first — it sets the allowable basis, the inspection level and who signs the drawing.

Criticality is decided by the consequence of failure, not by how hard the part is to make. Assign it at concept stage; retrofitting it after release triggers re-analysis and re-inspection of everything.

What criticality drives

ClassAllowable basisInspectionApproval
Safety-critical / fracture-criticalA-basis, damage tolerance100% NDT, FAI, serialisedIndependent check + design authority
Mission-criticalA- or B-basis by load pathNDT on critical features, FAIDesign authority
StandardB-basis or spec minimumSample inspectionNormal route

Your company's classes and their consequences will differ in detail — this is the shape, not the rule.

DFMEA, done usefully

  1. List functions, not parts. “Contain pressure”, “maintain clamp”, “locate within 0.1”.
  2. For each function, list how it fails and what happens next.
  3. Score severity independently of likelihood — a rare catastrophic mode is still catastrophic.
  4. For every high-severity line, name the design feature or test that controls it.
TRAP Single-point failures hidden by an assumed redundancy. Two seals in series with no way of testing the inner one is one seal plus a placebo. See Sealing strategy.

ZONE 14

Allowables & statistical basis

An allowable is a statistical statement with a basis, a temperature and a direction — a bare number is untraceable.

Quoting a typical value into a margin calculation is the quiet way to lose a design review.

BasisMeansUse when
A-basis99% of population exceeds, 95% confidenceSingle load path
B-basis90% exceeds, 95% confidenceRedundant load path, where permitted
S-basisSpecification minimum, no statistical backingUsually treated as A-basis — check your spec
TypicalMean of test dataNever in a margin

Knockdowns before the allowable is yours

  • Grain direction — short-transverse can be 10–20% below longitudinal in thick wrought product, with much lower elongation.
  • Section thickness — quench rate falls with thickness; heavy sections don't reach the thin-section allowable.
  • Welds — joint efficiency from the code and procedure qualification, not the parent metal.
  • Temperature and time — short-time and long-time allowables are different curves.
  • Process — additive and casting allowables are tied to the qualified process and supplier.
DESIGN RULE Keep basis, temperature, direction and product form in the same cell as the number. “σ = 880 MPa” on its own will be queried at every review until someone finds where it came from.
⚠ Screening guidance from general practice. Ranges are typical, not allowables — confirm against the governing standard, your programme specification and company procedures before anything reaches a released drawing.

Coatings & surface treatment

Every coating changes dimension, friction, fatigue or conductivity — state which you're accepting.

TreatmentForCosts you
Sulphuric anodiseCorrosion, paint base on AlDimension growth, fatigue debit, insulates
Hard anodiseWear on AlLarge fatigue debit, growth about half outward, brittle on edges
Chromic anodiseCorrosion with smaller fatigue debitHexavalent chromium — REACH restricted
Conversion coatingCorrosion, conductive, paint baseThin protection; hexavalent being replaced by trivalent
Zn-Ni platingSteel corrosion, cadmium replacementHydrogen embrittlement risk on high-strength steel
Electroless nickelUniform wear and corrosion layerFatigue debit; hardness varies with heat treatment
PassivationStainless steel corrosionNearly free — but must be specified
Dry film lubricantAnti-galling on threadsFriction changes your torque-preload relationship
Shot peeningFatigue lifeSurface roughness; needs intensity and coverage control
TRAP Plating high-strength steel — roughly above 1000 MPa tensile — introduces hydrogen that causes delayed brittle fracture, sometimes days after assembly. A de-embrittlement bake within a short time window after plating is mandatory. Specify it on the drawing with its governing standard, such as ASTM B850.

Drawing notes this zone requires

  • Whether dimensions apply before or after treatment.
  • Masking for threads, sealing faces, bonding points and electrical contact areas.
  • Any change in torque for coated or lubricated fasteners.

ZONE 21

Load paths & joint architecture

Trace each force from where it enters to where it leaves before any CAD; if you can't, the structure can't either.

Every structural problem in review is a load path problem in disguise. Sketch it by hand, per load case, with arrows.

Rules the load path obeys whether you like it or not

  • Load goes to stiffness. In parallel paths, the stiffer one carries more, regardless of which you intended to carry it.
  • Offsets create bending. Any eccentricity between where load arrives and where it's reacted becomes a moment. Moments make thin parts heavy.
  • Joints are discontinuities. Every joint is a change in stiffness and a stress raiser. Fewer joints in the primary path is almost always better.
  • Thermal loads are self-reacting. They never show up in the external free-body, which is exactly why they get missed.

Prying in tension flanges

When the bolt line sits outboard of the wall, the flange levers about its outer edge and the bolt sees more than its share of the applied load. The extra is the prying force, and on a flexible flange it can add tens of percent to the bolt load.

DESIGN RULE Keep the bolt circle as close to the wall as tool access allows, and make the flange stiff enough that it doesn't lever. Thickening the flange usually beats upsizing the bolts.
TRAP Lap joints carry secondary bending from the offset between the two sheets' mid-planes. Single-lap shear joints fail earlier than a pure shear calculation predicts for exactly this reason.

Joint architecture

IN ONE LINE Choose the joint type by what must come apart, seal and be inspected — mass comes after.

Joint choice locks in more mass, cost and risk than any detail decision that follows. Decide it explicitly against the requirements.

JointSeparableSeals wellStrengthsWatch
Bolted flangeYesYesRobust, inspectable, standard methodsMass, prying, preload loss
Radial pin / boltYesSeparate seal neededLow mass on thin cylindersBearing, net section, hole out-of-round
Threaded closureYesSeparate seal neededCompact, few partsGalling, thread root stress, torque control
Retaining ringYesSeparate seal neededVery compactGroove capacity, ring dishing
WeldedNoYesLightest, no leak pathHAZ knockdown, NDT access, distortion
BondedNoSometimesSpreads load, joins dissimilar materialsPeel, process control, inspection is hard
TRAP Welding a joint that must be opened for inspection, refurbishment or failure investigation. Ask who needs to get inside, and when, before choosing a permanent joint.
DESIGN RULE Separate the locating function from the clamping function. A spigot or dowels locate; bolts clamp. Bolts in clearance holes are not a location feature.
⚠ Screening guidance from general practice. Ranges are typical, not allowables — confirm against the governing standard, your programme specification and company procedures before anything reaches a released drawing.
CHECK ALONGSIDE
ZONE 22

Envelope, access & assembly

Reserve space for tools, hands and inspection probes, not just for parts.

The envelope a part needs in service is smaller than the envelope it needs to be assembled, torqued, inspected and taken apart. Design to the second.

Check every fastener for

  • Socket clearance — the socket's outside diameter, not the bolt head, sets the minimum pitch from walls. Check against the actual tool you'll use.
  • Torque wrench path — the wrench length and the swing it needs. A fastener you can reach but not torque to spec is an uncontrolled preload.
  • Insertion path — the bolt has to get into the hole from somewhere. Count its full length.
  • Visibility — the assembler must be able to see the fastener seat and any locking feature.

Beyond fasteners

  • Assembly order: can every part get to its position with the others already in place?
  • Lifting points and centre of gravity for anything you can't lift by hand.
  • Inspection access for the CMM probe, borescope or NDT transducer.
  • Thermal clearance at the extremes — parts that fit at 20°C can touch at the operating limit.
  • Harness and pipe routes with their bend radii, not as thin lines.
DESIGN RULE Model the critical tools as solids in the assembly. It takes ten minutes and catches problems that otherwise turn up on the shop floor.
⚠ Screening guidance from general practice. Ranges are typical, not allowables — confirm against the governing standard, your programme specification and company procedures before anything reaches a released drawing.

ZONE 29

Hand-calc library

Hand calcs bound the answer before FEA — if the two disagree by more than about 20%, find out why before trusting either.

Pressure-loaded shells

thin cylinder (r/t > ~10): σ_hoop = p·r / t σ_axial = p·r / (2t) thin sphere: σ = p·r / (2t) thick cylinder, bore (Lamé): σ_θ = p·(r_o² + r_i²) / (r_o² − r_i²)

Flat plates — uniform pressure, radius a

clamped edge, max at edge: σ = 3·p·a² / (4·t²) simply supported, max at centre: σ = 3·(3+ν)·p·a² / (8·t²)

Real flange-to-plate joints lie between these two bounds. Use both.

Beams and columns

bending: σ = M·c / I cantilever tip load: δ = F·L³ / (3·E·I) Euler buckling: P_cr = π²·E·I / (K·L)²

Thin cylinders in axial compression

classical: σ_cr ≈ 0.605 · E · t / r (ν = 0.3)
TRAP Classical shell buckling is badly unconservative. Real cylinders buckle well below it because of imperfections. NASA SP-8007 knockdown factors are substantially below 1 and fall as r/t rises. Never use the classical value unfactored.

Fasteners and lugs

metric tensile stress area: A_s = (π/4) · (d − 0.9382·p)² bearing: σ_br = P / (d·t) shear-out: τ ≈ P / (2·e·t) e = edge distance to hole centre

Thermal

fully constrained: σ = E · α · ΔT

Steel fully constrained through 100 K reaches roughly 240 MPa — before any mechanical load.

Stress concentration

Net-section stress × K_t from Peterson's charts. K_t matters for fatigue and brittle materials; ductile static failure is usually governed by net section.

ZONE 30

Differential expansion

Absolute growth rarely breaks anything. Differential growth between parts that are bolted, pinned, fitted or sealed together does.

DECIDE WHETHER EACH JOINT IS CONSTRAINED OR FREE — AND DRAW IT THAT WAY Joints meant to slide but bolted solid are a classic source of cracking at the outermost fastener. The calculator below gives the three numbers that matter: the mismatch, what it does to a fit, and what it does to bolt preload.

Pair and temperature

Result

—

Expansion coefficients used

Materialα ×10⁻⁶/KE GPaPairs badly with
differential at a joint: Δ = (α₁ − α₂) · L · ΔT fit change: Δc = D · (α_outer − α_inner) · ΔT fully constrained stress: σ = E · α · ΔT preload change: ΔF = −Δ / (δ_bolt + δ_joint), δ_bolt = L / (E_b · A_s), δ_joint = δ_bolt / ratio
TRANSIENTS BEAT STEADY STATE During heating, thin sections lead thick ones. A flange and its bolts at different temperatures for a few seconds can see a larger mismatch than either steady state. Check the transient case with the Transient thermal zone, not just the end points.
THE FIT HAS TO WORK AT BOTH ENDS An aluminium housing on a steel bearing gains clearance hot and loses it cold. Size the interference at the hot end, then check assembly stress at the cold end.
LONG BOLTS ARE FORGIVING For the same mismatch, a longer, more compliant bolt changes preload less. Raising the grip ratio is often cheaper than changing material.
ELASTOMERS GROW TEN TIMES MORE Seal compounds expand roughly ten times as much as the metal around them. Gland fill has to be checked at the hottest point, at minimum groove volume.
⚠ Linear α at a single representative value. α varies with temperature, strongly so below about −100°C — use the Cryogenic design zone for cold cases. Stiffness ratio is an input, not a calculation; VDI 2230 gives the joint compliance properly.

Where it bites

  • Bolt preload — short grip, dissimilar materials, large ΔT. Rising preload can yield the bolt; falling preload opens the joint.
  • Interference fits — an aluminium housing loses interference hot. Size at the hot end, check stress at the cold end.
  • Large flanges — radial differential forces bolts into shear and fretting. Use slots, a spigot or a deliberate sliding joint.
  • Transients — during heating, thin sections lead thick ones. Transient gradients can exceed the steady-state case.
DESIGN RULE Decide early whether each joint is constrained or free, and draw it that way. Joints meant to slide but bolted solid are a classic source of cracking at the outermost fastener.
CHECK ALONGSIDE
ZONE 31

Margin of safety policy

A margin is only meaningful if load, factor and allowable are a consistent set — yield with yield, ultimate with ultimate.

MS = allowable / (FoS × limit load) − 1 pass when MS ≥ 0

Errors behind most review findings

  1. Mixed pairs — yield allowable against ultimate load. Run yield and ultimate as separate lines.
  2. Wrong basis — typical or room-temperature values in a hot, single-load-path check.
  3. Missing factors — see below.
  4. Stacked conservatism — pessimistic load × allowable × model gives a heavy part and a margin nobody believes. Record where conservatism sits so it can be removed deliberately.

Additional factors to look for in your spec

FactorApplies to
Fitting factorJoints and fittings, where stress state is uncertain
Bearing factorBearing at fastener holes with clearance or vibration
Casting factorCast parts, linked to inspection level
Weld factorWelded joints, linked to procedure and inspection
Model uncertainty factorUnvalidated analysis methods

These multiply onto the basic factor. Missing a required one makes every margin downstream wrong.

Combined loads

Use interaction equations for combined loading — for example fastener tension with shear. The form varies by spec (linear, quadratic or mixed exponents). Use the one your spec mandates; NASA-STD-5020 covers fasteners for spaceflight.

Reporting

One row per failure mode per load case: load case, failure mode, allowable with basis and temperature, factors with source, MS, analysis reference.

DESIGN RULE A margin above roughly 0.5 on a mass-driven part is a finding, not a success. Either the part is heavy or the load case is wrong.
Factor values are not held here. Yield, ultimate, proof and special factors come from your programme specification or governing code.
⚠ Screening guidance from general practice. Ranges are typical, not allowables — confirm against the governing standard, your programme specification and company procedures before anything reaches a released drawing.
CHECK ALONGSIDE
ZONE 38

Test correlation

Write the predictions and pass criteria before the test, and instrument where the model is least certain.

Before the test

  1. Record predicted strains, deflections or frequencies at every instrument location.
  2. Set correlation criteria now. Common targets: strains within about 10–15% at significant locations; primary mode frequencies within about 5% with MAC ≥ 0.9. Confirm against your verification spec.
  3. Place gauges where the model is least certain, not just where it's easy.

Instrumentation

  • Rosettes where principal directions are unknown; uniaxial gauges only where they're certain.
  • Avoid steep gradients unless deliberately measuring a peak — a gauge averages over its length.
  • Temperature-compensate gauges and record temperature alongside.
  • Calibrated, traceable load cells and transducers.
  • Zero readings before load; check return to zero after.

After the test

If results fall outside criteria, find the physical reason — a stiffer joint, a different boundary condition, a material property. Update the model on that basis, then re-predict.

TRAP Tuning parameters until the model matches, with no physical justification. A model forced to match one test predicts the next one no better than before.
⚠ Screening guidance from general practice. Ranges are typical, not allowables — confirm against the governing standard, your programme specification and company procedures before anything reaches a released drawing.
CHECK ALONGSIDE
ZONE 39

Storage, ageing & surveillance

Hardware that sits on a shelf for years is still changing — seals set, adhesives oxidise, preload relaxes, coatings degrade. Plan for it, and test for it honestly.

ACCELERATED AGEING ASSUMES ONE MECHANISM An Arrhenius extrapolation is only valid if the same degradation mechanism governs at the test temperature and in service. Push the test temperature too high and you age the part by a different chemistry — then extrapolate the wrong answer with great precision.

Arrhenius equivalence

Mean kinetic temperature

Result

—
acceleration factor: AF = exp[ (Ea / R) · (1/T_service − 1/T_test) ] T in kelvin, R = 8.314 J/mol·K equivalent service: t_service = AF · t_test mean kinetic temp: T_MKT = (Ea/R) / −ln[ (1/n) · Σ exp(−Ea / (R·T_i)) ]

What ages, and what to watch

ItemMechanismDesign response
Elastomer sealsCompression set, oxidation, loss of low-temperature resilienceBudget set into minimum squeeze; record cure date; surveillance samples
Adhesive and bonded jointsMoisture uptake, plasticisation, interface degradationHumidity-aged allowables; protect the bond line edge
Bolted jointsPreload relaxation, embedment, creep of coatings and gasketsLong grips, no soft layers in the clamp, retorque policy if allowed
Coatings and platingsBreakdown at edges and damage, galvanic attackCoat the cathode too; inspect edges and fastener heads
Lubricants and greasesDrying, separation, migration onto sealsCompatible with the elastomer; specify quantity, not "lightly"
THE AVERAGE TEMPERATURE IS THE WRONG AVERAGE Ageing rate rises exponentially with temperature, so hot days count for far more than cold nights. A store that cycles between 10 and 40°C ages hardware faster than a constant 25°C store. Use mean kinetic temperature, which weights the hot readings properly.
THICK SECTIONS AGE FROM THE OUTSIDE IN At high test temperatures, oxygen is consumed near the surface faster than it can diffuse inward. The skin ages and the core doesn't — a pattern that never happens in service. Thick elastomer and polymer parts need modest test temperatures or a check for this effect.
Ea IS A PROPERTY OF THE MECHANISM, NOT THE MATERIAL NAME Typical values for polymer oxidation fall broadly in the 50–120 kJ/mol range, and the answer is very sensitive to it. Measure it from at least three test temperatures — the slope of ln(life) against 1/T — rather than assuming it.
SURVEILLANCE BEATS PREDICTION Hold back representative samples stored with the hardware, and test them on a schedule. A prediction tells you what should have happened; surveillance tells you what did.
BOND AND LINER AGEING HAS ITS OWN TOOL Case-bond and liner property drift with age is modelled in the Propellant grain zone.
⚠ Single-mechanism Arrhenius model. ISO 11346 covers lifetime estimation for rubbers properly. This zone covers seals, adhesives, coatings and joints — not energetic materials, whose ageing sits with your energetics specialists.
ZONE 41

Datums, position & form in practice

Datums should mirror how the part is located in its assembly — primary on the largest, most stable functional contact.

Degrees of freedom removed

DatumFeatureRemoves
PrimaryPlane (3 points of contact)1 translation, 2 rotations
SecondaryPlane (2 points) or axisFurther translation and rotation
TertiaryPlane (1 point) or slotRemaining clocking

Choosing them

  1. Primary: the face that seats the part in its assembly — usually the largest mating face.
  2. Secondary: the feature that locates it — spigot, bore or dowel hole.
  3. Tertiary: the feature that clocks it — second dowel, slot or keyway.

Datums must be the same features, in the same order, as the mating part and the ICD.

Datum targets

For castings, forgings and large thin parts, use datum targets — specific points, lines or areas — so the part is fixtured identically every time, before its faces are machined.

TRAP Datuming on a face that's convenient to the machinist instead of functional in the assembly. The part passes inspection and then doesn't fit, because it was measured in a reference frame it never uses.

Position & MMC

IN ONE LINE Use MMC where the feature only has to assemble; use RFS where it locates or seals.

Position defines a tolerance zone — usually cylindrical — for a feature's axis, relative to datums. Applied at MMC, it gains bonus tolerance as the feature departs from its maximum material size.

Fastener formulas

floating fastener (clearance holes in both parts): T = H − F fixed fastener (one part tapped or pinned): T = (H − F) / 2 each part, equal split H = MMC hole size F = MMC fastener size T = position tolerance at MMC

Example — M8 bolt, ⌀9.0 clearance holes: floating gives ⌀1.0 at each hole; if one part is tapped, ⌀0.5 at each.

Projected tolerance zone

For tapped holes and press-fit pins, the position error that matters is where the mating fastener sits, above the surface — not inside the hole. A slight tilt inside the hole becomes a large offset at the mating part. Specify a projected zone (Ⓟ) with a height equal to the mating part's thickness.

TRAP Fixed-fastener patterns without a projected zone. Parts pass inspection individually and won't assemble.

Patterns

Composite position separates the pattern's location to the datums (loose) from the feature-to-feature spacing within the pattern (tight). Use it where the bolt pattern must match a mating part closely but can float as a group.

Flatness

IN ONE LINE For a sealing face, flatness comes from the squeeze budget — and the measurement method can move the number.

Flatness controls one surface against itself: two parallel planes that float to best fit. It constrains form only.

Choose it from the function

ApplicationFlatnessRaDriven by
Face-seal gland face0.050.8Minimum squeeze across the seal
Metal-to-metal bolted flange0.1–0.23.2Rocking, preload uniformity
Datum feature, precision0.020.4Repeatability of measurement
General machined face0.33.2Process capability

Typical starting points — derive the real value from the seal squeeze or joint stiffness it serves.

TRAP Free state versus restrained. Flatness is inspected unclamped by default. A thin flange that pulls flat under bolt load will be rejected even though it seals perfectly. Either add a free-state note with a realistic value, or define the restrained condition — don't just tighten the number.

Measurement method moves the result

The tolerance is defined by the minimum-zone condition. A least-squares fit, the default on many CMM programs, always reports flatness equal to or larger than minimum zone — so it can reject conforming parts, never the reverse. Agree the fitting method and the point density with inspection before release. A handful of points on an annular face proves very little.

Profile of a surface

IN ONE LINE Profile with datums controls size, form, orientation and location in one frame — use it on any surface that isn't a simple feature of size.
  • Profile of a surface — a three-dimensional zone around the true profile.
  • Profile of a line — the same, applied cross-section by cross-section.

Datum referencing changes what it controls

AppliedControls
No datumForm and size only — the zone floats
Orientation datumForm, size and orientation
Full datum reference frameForm, size, orientation and location

Zone placement

Default is bilateral and equal about the true profile. For unequal zones, ASME uses the U modifier; ISO uses UZ with an offset. These are not interchangeable notations — use the one your governing standard defines.

DESIGN RULE On complex surfaces — blends, aero shapes, freeform — profile replaces coordinate ± tolerances entirely. Coordinate tolerances on curved surfaces create square zones that don't match the function.

Runout & concentricity

IN ONE LINE Use runout for rotating features; avoid concentricity, which is hard to measure and was removed from ASME Y14.5-2018.
ControlWhat it checksUse
Circular runoutEach cross-section as the part rotatesWobble at individual sections
Total runoutThe whole surface as the part rotatesOverall rotating fit, seal surfaces on shafts
Position (RFS) of an axisAxis location to a datum axisCoaxial features without rotation measurement
ConcentricityMedian points of a featureRemoved in ASME 2018 — avoid

ISO retains coaxiality, which is effectively position of an axis. ASME removed concentricity and symmetry in the 2018 edition because they were rarely measured as defined.

Datum axis

For shafts supported in two bearings, establish the axis from both journals together: datum A-B. A single short datum feature gives a poorly defined axis.

TRAP Runout checked in V-blocks on a lobed datum feature. Out-of-round datums produce false readings. Use centres or a roundness machine for tight runout.

Runout includes form error — it's a composite control. A part can fail runout from roundness alone.

Measurement & gauging

Agree how each critical characteristic will be measured before release — an unmeasurable tolerance becomes a dispute at goods-in.

Measurement capability

  • Uncertainty — aim for ≤10% of tolerance; 25% is a common floor.
  • Decision rules — ISO 14253-1 reduces the acceptance zone by the measurement uncertainty. Tight tolerances lose a large share of themselves to the gauge.
  • Gauge R&R — <10% of tolerance acceptable, 10–30% marginal, >30% unacceptable.

Method by characteristic

CharacteristicUsual method
Position, profileCMM; functional gauge for position at MMC
FlatnessCMM minimum-zone, or surface plate and indicator
Bore sizeBore gauge, air gauge
Roundness, runoutRoundness machine, or centres and indicator
Surface finishStylus profilometer — state cutoff
ThreadsGo/no-go thread gauges

Temperature

Dimensions are defined at 20°C. An aluminium part 200 mm long measured at 25°C reads about 0.023 mm long — more than a tight tolerance. Soak parts in the measurement room, or compensate.

TRAP The CMM program defines the measurement. Two labs measuring the same feature with different fits, filters or point densities get different answers, and both are “right”. Specify the method for critical features.

Sealing strategy

Decide where the leak path is and how many barriers cross it — then make every barrier testable on its own.

Sealing strategy is decided at layout, not at detail. Once the joint architecture is frozen, you only get to pick the O-ring size.

Face or radial

ArrangementToleratesSensitive to
Face (axial) sealRadial movement, diametral mismatchJoint gapping, flatness, preload loss
Radial (bore) sealAxial movement, joint gappingBore dilation, eccentricity, extrusion gap

If the joint is likely to open slightly under load, a radial seal keeps sealing while a face seal unloads. That single fact decides a lot of layouts.

Seal families by duty

FamilyTemperatureReuseUse when
Elastomer O-ringCompound-limitedUsually replaceDefault — cheap, forgiving
O-ring + backup ringCompound-limitedReplaceHigher pressure, larger gaps
Spring-energised PTFEWideSometimesDynamic, chemically aggressive, low friction
Metallic C- or E-ringHighNoBeyond elastomer limits; needs fine finish and high load
Flat gasketMaterial-limitedNoAvoid in structural joints — creep kills preload

Redundant seals

TRAP Two seals in series with nothing between them. You can't tell whether the primary is working, and the trapped volume between them can pressurise during a slow leak or a temperature rise. Put a test port between the seals, or don't claim redundancy.
DESIGN RULE Every claimed barrier needs its own leak check. A redundant seal you can't test separately only proves the pair works on the day — not that you still have a spare.

ZONE 49

Locking & retention

Preload is the primary lock — locking features only stop a joint coming apart once it has already loosened.

Retaining rings

Capacity is usually limited by the groove, not the ring. The groove edge yields in the softer housing material, or the ring dishes if the abutting part has a chamfer or radius.

  • Keep the groove edge sharp and the abutting face square. A chamfer on the abutting part can cut capacity drastically.
  • Check groove edge yield in aluminium housings — it governs well before ring shear.
  • For high thrust, use a shoulder, a thrust collar or a threaded retainer instead.

Locking methods ranked against transverse vibration

MethodEffectNotes
Adequate preload, long gripBestPrevents the slip that causes loosening
Lockwire / safety cablePrevents lossAllows some rotation; inspectable
Wedge-locking washersGoodCheck compatibility with surface coatings
Prevailing-torque nutsModerateReuse limits; check running torque on reuse
Anaerobic thread-lockerGood when curedTemperature limit, cure on passive metals needs primer
Split spring washersNegligibleFlatten at preload — don't rely on them
TRAP Thread-locking compound changes friction and therefore preload for a given torque. If you add it, the torque value must change too.
⚠ Screening guidance from general practice. Ranges are typical, not allowables — confirm against the governing standard, your programme specification and company procedures before anything reaches a released drawing.
CHECK ALONGSIDE
ZONE 53

Process selection & additive

Choose the process from quantity, material and the tightest feature — then design everything else to that process's natural capability.

ProcessTypical toleranceRa µmFits
CNC milling±0.05, ±0.01 precision0.8–3.2Prismatic parts, low–medium volume
CNC turning±0.0250.4–3.2Rotational parts
Grinding±0.0050.1–0.8Bearing and seal surfaces
Wire EDM±0.0050.4–1.6Hard materials, sharp internal profiles
Investment casting≈±0.13 per 25 mm1.6–3.2Complex shapes, medium volume
Sand casting±0.5–26.3–25Large, low volume, needs machining
Closed-die forging±0.5, machined after—Strength, grain flow, volume
Sheet metal±0.1–0.25mill finishThin structure, brackets
Metal additive (LPBF)±0.1–0.26–15 as-builtInternal geometry, consolidation

Plate, forging or bar

Machining from plate is fast to obtain but cuts across grain flow. Forgings put the grain where the load is and carry better short-transverse properties, but lead times are long and tooling is costly. Your allowables must match the form actually procured.

DESIGN RULE Only the features that need precision should get it. One tight tolerance on a part doesn't justify tight tolerances on the rest.

Additive suitability

IN ONE LINE Use additive where it removes assemblies or enables internal geometry — not to make a machinable part more expensively.

Good and poor candidates

GoodPoor
Internal channels and passagesSimple prismatic parts
Consolidating several parts and joints into oneLarge flat sealing faces as-built
Lattices, topology-optimised bracketsHigh-volume parts
Low-volume complex partsParts with no process qualification route

Laser powder bed fusion rules of thumb

  • Overhangs steeper than about 45° from the build plate self-support; shallower needs support.
  • Horizontal holes up to roughly 6–8 mm can self-support; larger need teardrop shapes or support.
  • Minimum wall roughly 0.3–0.5 mm, machine-dependent.
  • Internal channels need powder exit routes and inspection access.
  • Build orientation sets anisotropy — properties in the build direction usually differ.

Post-processing is not optional

  • Stress relieve before removal from the plate.
  • HIP to close internal porosity for fatigue-loaded parts.
  • Machine every sealing face, thread and datum.
  • CT or other volumetric inspection for internal features.
TRAP Allowables belong to the qualified machine, powder and parameter set — not to the alloy. Change the supplier or the parameters and the data no longer applies.
⚠ Screening guidance from general practice. Ranges are typical, not allowables — confirm against the governing standard, your programme specification and company procedures before anything reaches a released drawing.

ZONE 57

Leak testing

Every seal leaks at some rate. The requirement is a number, a method that can see it, and a test that isn't fooled by temperature.

“NO LEAKS” IS NOT A REQUIREMENT State the allowable leak rate, the test gas, the pressure, the method and its sensitivity. Without all five, a pass means only that the test couldn't see anything.

Pressure decay test

Result

—

Unit converter

Method by sensitivity

MethodApproximate sensitivity mbar·L/sGood forWatch
Bubble immersion / spray≈10⁻³ – 10⁻⁴Locating gross leaksOperator dependent; contaminates
Pressure decay≈10⁻³ – 10⁻⁴Integral check of a whole assemblyTemperature, volume — see calculator
Helium sniffer≈10⁻⁶ – 10⁻⁷Locating leaks on pressurised partsBackground helium, sniffer distance
Helium accumulation (hood)≈10⁻⁷ – 10⁻⁸Integral rate of a pressurised partHood volume and soak time
Helium hard vacuum≈10⁻⁹ and belowHighest sensitivity integral testWrong pressure direction for some seals
TEMPERATURE SWAMPS PRESSURE DECAY Gas pressure follows absolute temperature. At 11 bar absolute, a 0.1 K drift moves pressure by roughly 375 Pa — often more than the leak you are trying to see. Soak to equilibrium, log temperature, and correct for it or the test is measuring the weather.
TEST THE SEAL IN THE DIRECTION IT WORKS A vacuum test loads a seal the opposite way to service pressure. Some seals — lip seals, pressure-energised designs — leak backwards and seal forwards. Make sure the test pressure direction matches the service direction, or justify the difference.
TRACER GAS LEAK RATES DO NOT EQUAL SERVICE LEAK RATES Helium is small and fast. Converting a helium rate to a service fluid rate depends on the flow regime through the leak path. Specify the requirement as a helium rate at stated conditions, and keep the conversion argument separate.
EVERY CLAIMED BARRIER NEEDS ITS OWN TEST With two seals in series, a port between them is the only way to prove each is working. Without one, the second seal is untestable — see Sealing strategy.
⚠ Pressure decay uses Q = V·ΔP/Δt with an ideal-gas temperature correction. Sensitivities are typical orders of magnitude; the governing figures come from your test procedure and calibrated standard leaks.
ZONE 59

Certificates & traceability

A datasheet typical value is marketing; a certificate against a specification is evidence.

Material certificates — EN 10204

TypeContentValidated by
2.1Declaration of compliance, no resultsManufacturer
2.2Non-specific test resultsManufacturer
3.1Specific results for the delivered batchManufacturer's independent inspector
3.2As 3.1, also verifiedPurchaser's representative or third party

Aerospace structural parts normally need 3.1 at minimum. Check your spec.

Check every certificate for

  • Specification, issue and condition match the drawing.
  • Heat or cast number traceable to the material received.
  • Test specimen orientation and location relevant to your load direction.
  • Results from the delivered batch, not historic data.
TRAP Counterfeit and suspect parts, fasteners especially. Check head markings against the certificate and buy from approved sources. A certificate that doesn't match the markings is a non-conformance.

ZONE 62

Drawing frame & note library

The title block declares the rules the whole drawing is read by — governing standard, projection, units and general tolerances.

Title block must state

FieldWhy
Governing standard and issueSets how every symbol is interpreted
Projection symbolFirst angle in UK and Europe, third angle in the US — never assume
UnitsMillimetres unless stated; state it anyway
General tolerancesApply to every untoleranced dimension
Default surface finishApplies to every surface not otherwise marked
Material, specification and conditionIncluding heat treatment
Criticality classificationDrives inspection and approval
Export control markingLegal requirement where applicable
Mass, scale, sheet n of m, revisionHousekeeping that gets audited

ISO and ASME read size differently

Under ISO 8015 the default is the independency principle: a size tolerance doesn't control form. A shaft can be in size and still be bent. Apply the envelope requirement Ⓔ where form must be inside size.

Under ASME Y14.5 the default is Rule #1: size controls form via the envelope. The same drawing can be read differently depending on which applies.

TRAP General tolerances from ISO 2768 on a functional feature. They suit non-critical geometry but don't express any function. Tolerance every functional feature explicitly.

Note library

IN ONE LINE Every note is a requirement — specific, verifiable and stated once.

Notes worth standardising

Fill the brackets from your specs. These show the shape of a good note, not your company's wording.

  1. Interpret drawing per [governing standard and issue].
  2. Remove burrs. Break sharp edges [range] unless otherwise specified.
  3. Dimensions apply [before / after] surface treatment.
  4. Mask threads and surfaces marked [symbol] from treatment.
  5. Tighten to [torque] using [lubricant], friction coefficient assumed [range].
  6. Bake for hydrogen embrittlement relief per [spec] within [time] of plating.
  7. Mark part and serial number per [spec] at location shown, by [method]. No impression stamping on [class] parts.
  8. Clean to [cleanliness level] per [spec] before assembly.
  9. Inspect [features] by [method] to [acceptance standard and class].

Notes that don't work

NoteProblem
“Break all sharp edges”No size — unenforceable
“Clean before assembly”No level or method
“Finish to suit”Delegates a design decision to the shop
“Torque to standard values”Which standard, which lubricant?
DESIGN RULE State each requirement once. A torque value in a note and a different one on the view creates a non-conformance whichever is followed.

ZONE 63

Revision control & sign-off

If the change keeps parts interchangeable it's a revision; if not, it's a new part number.

Revision or new part number

ChangeInterchangeable?Action
Clarify a note, fix a typoYesRevision
Relax a tolerance, parts still fitYesRevision
Change material gradeUsually notNew part number
Change a mating featureNoNew part number
Add a feature old parts lackUsually notNew part number

Practice

  • Every revision references its change record and lists the zones affected.
  • Avoid revision letters that read like numbers — I, O, Q, S, X and Z are commonly excluded.
  • Decide whether the drawing or the model is the master, and say so on the drawing. Model-based definition is legitimate, but only if one source is authoritative.
  • Mark superseded copies clearly, or remove them from use.
TRAP Updating the model without re-releasing the drawing, or the reverse. The shop builds whichever they have.

Sign-off route

IN ONE LINE Each signatory checks something different — if two check the same thing, a gap exists somewhere else.
RoleChecks
DrawnComplete and matches the model
CheckedDrawing practice, GD&T, every feature defined once and unambiguously
StressMargins exist and reference released analysis
ManufacturingProducible with the intended process and tooling
QualityEvery requirement can be measured or verified
Design authorityMeets the requirements; approves release

Higher criticality adds independent checks. See Criticality & DFMEA.

Checker's short list

  1. Is every feature fully defined, with nothing double-dimensioned?
  2. Does each datum scheme match its mating part and ICD?
  3. Is every functional feature explicitly toleranced?
  4. Are material, condition, treatments and notes complete?
  5. Can each characteristic be measured?
TRAP Checking in the live CAD model rather than the released drawing. The checker must sign what will actually be issued.

ZONE 64

Archive & export control

Release in a neutral, frozen format carrying its export control marking — the native CAD file is not the record.

Archive formats

ContentFormatWhy
DrawingsPDF/A (ISO 19005)Self-contained, designed for long-term readability
3D models with PMISTEP AP242 (ISO 10303-242)Neutral, carries tolerances and annotation
Native CADKeep, but not as the recordBecomes unreadable as software versions move on

Retain records for the period your contract requires — often the life of the product plus a defined number of years. Store checksums so integrity can be shown.

Export control

  • Classify the technical data against the UK Strategic Export Control Lists — military and dual-use — before it leaves your organisation.
  • Mark drawings and file metadata with the classification.
  • Sending technology by email, cloud share or hand-carried drive counts as an export.
  • US-origin content can bring ITAR or EAR obligations on top of UK controls.
  • Exports need the right licence — SIEL, OIEL or an applicable OGEL. Your export compliance team decides; the designer marks.
TRAP Sending a drawing to a supplier or overseas colleague without checking its classification. The liability sits with the sender, not the recipient.

Weibull reliability

Life data in, failure behaviour out — shape, characteristic life and B-lives. Zero or one failure switches to Weibayes, which is how a set of successful tests demonstrates reliability.

Typical uses: seal or valve cycles to leak, fatigue coupons, fastener reuse, connector mating cycles. Analyse one failure mode at a time.

Monte Carlo uncertainty

Give each input a distribution, write the result as an expression, and see how often it crosses a limit. Ranks design options; doesn't certify one.

NameDist.P1P2P3

normal: mean, sd · uniform: min, max · triangular: min, mode, max · const: value

Regression with prediction intervals

The bench answers "what drives this?". This answers "where will the next one land, and how sure is that?" — with the residuals on show so a bad model can't hide.

Example: strength against temperature. For S-N data use the power model with cycles as x and stress as y.
